A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket chosen by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, the map has a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions by chaining: each bucket holds a linked list or tree of entries that share that bucket. The map inserts the new entry at the bucket, then searches the chain during lookups.

Open addressing handles collisions differently. It probes a sequence of alternative slots—linear, quadratic, or double hashing—until it finds an empty one. Lookups follow the same probe sequence.

Load factor governs performance. Chained maps slow down as chains lengthen; open-addressing maps degrade as clusters form. A high load factor triggers a resize: the map allocates a larger array, rehashes every entry, and redistributes them into fresh buckets.

Java's `HashMap` uses chaining and converts long chains into balanced trees. Python's `dict` uses open addressing with a probe sequence derived from the hash. The choice trades memory against worst-case lookup time.

A database index is a separate structure that maps lookup values to row locations so the engine can find rows without scanning the whole table.

An index helps when the query filters, joins, or sorts on the indexed column. A B-tree index turns a full-table scan into a few page reads. A hash index speeds exact-match lookups but cannot support range queries.

An index hurts when it is unused, when writes are frequent, or when the query returns most of the table. Every insert, update, or delete must maintain the index, which costs writes and storage. A narrow, highly selective query benefits; a query that returns half the rows may spend more time traversing the index and fetching pages than scanning sequentially.

Indexes also hurt when they are redundant, when statistics are stale, or when the optimizer chooses the wrong plan. Covering indexes help only if the query asks for columns the index contains. Composite indexes work only for leading-column predicates; a query on the second column walks the whole index.

The right index matches the query shape, selectivity, and write load. The wrong index is extra cost with no payoff.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions on shared data.

A race condition happens when two threads read and write the same memory at the same time. One thread may overwrite another's change, or both may read a stale value and act on it. The result depends on timing, so it varies from run to run.

A mutex is a lock. One thread acquires it before entering a critical section. While that thread holds the lock, other threads that try to acquire the same mutex block until it is released. Only one thread at a time passes through.

This turns concurrent access into serialized access around the protected data. It does not prevent bugs in the code inside the critical section; it only prevents two threads from entering that section together.

A mutex protects data, not code. The programmer must acquire the right mutex before touching the shared state and release it after. Locking the wrong mutex, or forgetting to lock at all, leaves the data exposed.

Deadlock is the common cost. Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2; thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Neither proceeds. Consistent lock ordering, or reducing the number of locks, prevents this.

A mutex is not free. Acquisition and release take time, and contention makes threads wait. A mutex held for a long time or around unnecessary work hurts performance. A mutex held too briefly or omitted hurts correctness.

A race condition is a bug where a program's result depends on the timing or order of concurrent operations.

Two threads run the same code. Both read a shared counter, add one, and write it back. Thread A reads 5. Before A writes, thread B reads 5 too. A writes 6. B writes 6. The counter should be 7; it is 6. The final value depends on which thread wins the race.

The bug is not in the arithmetic. It is in the gap between the read and the write, when another thread can step in.

A mutex fixes this by letting only one thread through the read-increment-write sequence at a time. Atomic operations fix it by making the read and write a single indivisible step.

Race conditions also appear in file systems, databases, and distributed systems. Anywhere two actors touch shared state without coordination, the outcome can shift with timing.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far from the CPU on a separate chip. Fetching a value from it takes hundreds of clock cycles. The cache is smaller memory built into or near the CPU. It can deliver data in a handful of cycles.

Programs tend to reuse data they just touched, and to access nearby memory next. The cache exploits both habits. It stores whole blocks, called cache lines, not single bytes. When the CPU reads one cell, the cache pulls in its neighbors too.

A hit occurs when the CPU finds the data in cache. A miss sends it to main memory and stalls the pipeline while the cache line arrives. A program with good locality—tight loops over compact arrays—hits often and runs fast. A program that jumps through scattered memory misses often and waits.

Caches form levels. L1 is smallest and fastest, often 32 or 64 kilobytes per core. L2 is larger and slower. L3 is shared across cores and slower still. The CPU checks L1, then L2, then L3, then RAM.

Writes complicate the design. A write-through cache updates both cache and memory immediately. A write-back cache updates only the cache and flushes the line to memory later, when it is evicted. Write-back is faster but requires tracking which lines are dirty.

False sharing hurts performance. Two cores write different variables that happen to live on the same cache line. Each write invalidates the other core's copy, forcing repeated fetches from a shared level. Padding variables onto separate lines fixes it.

Cache size and access pattern matter more than raw clock speed for many programs. A fast CPU with constant misses waits like a slow one.

A client sends `PUT /users/42` with the same payload twice. The first request creates or updates the record. The second request leaves the record in the same final state. The server does not apply the change twice.

`GET` and `HEAD` are naturally idempotent. They read state and do not change it.

`PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent by design. Deleting a resource twice leaves it deleted. Updating a resource to the same value twice leaves it at that value.

`POST` is usually not idempotent. A client that sends `POST /charges` twice may create two charges. The API must use explicit deduplication keys or tokens if it wants a `POST` to be safe to retry.

Idempotency matters for retries. Networks drop packets, clients time out, and responses get lost. A client that retries an idempotent call does not risk duplicate work. A client that retries a non-idempotent call needs a separate mechanism, such as an `Idempotency-Key` header, so the server recognizes the duplicate and returns the first result.

The server still processes the retry. It may log it, run validation, or return the same response. The protected property is the state change, not the traffic.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a hierarchy of servers.

A browser sends `example.com` to a recursive resolver, often run by the ISP or a public service like Cloudflare or Google. The resolver checks its cache. If it has the answer, it returns it.

If not, the resolver asks a root server. The root server does not know `example.com`, but it points the resolver to the server for the `.com` zone.

The resolver asks the `.com` server. That server points it to the authoritative server for `example.com`.

The resolver asks the authoritative server. That server returns the A record, which holds the IPv4 address, or the AAAA record for IPv6.

The resolver caches the result and sends the address back to the browser. The browser opens a TCP connection to that address.

Each step uses UDP for small queries and TCP for large ones. A record carries a TTL, which tells resolvers how long they may cache it before asking again.

CNAME records redirect to another name. MX records point to mail servers. NS records delegate authority to another server. The resolver follows these records until it finds the address.

A deadlock is a standoff where two or more threads each hold a lock and wait for another to release one.

Thread A locks the account table and waits for the transaction log. Thread B locks the transaction log and waits for the account table. Neither thread can proceed. Neither releases its lock. The program stalls.

One way to avoid it is to lock in a fixed order. Every thread that needs both resources must acquire the account table lock first, then the transaction log lock. Thread B would not take the log first; it would back up and take the account table. The circular wait disappears.

Other methods exist. A timeout can abandon a lock attempt and retry. Lock ordering, however, removes the cycle at the source.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket chosen by running the key through a hash function and reducing that hash to an index within the array of buckets. Two different keys can produce the same index; that event is a collision.

The two common responses to a collision are chaining and open addressing. Chaining keeps a linked list, tree, or other structure at each bucket. Every entry that hashes to the same index goes into that structure. Open addressing places the entry in another bucket within the same array, found by probing forward until an empty slot appears.

Load factor governs performance. As the ratio of stored entries to bucket count rises, collisions become more frequent. Most implementations resize the backing array and rehash every entry into the larger array once the load factor crosses a threshold, often around 0.75.

The hash function itself matters. A poor hash function clusters keys into a few buckets and defeats the array. A good one spreads keys evenly across the whole range. Many maps also mix the hash bits before reducing them, so that high-order bits influence low-order indices and break patterns in the key distribution.

A database index is a separate, smaller structure that points to rows in a table, built from one or more columns so the database can find matching rows without scanning the whole table.

An index helps when the query filters, sorts, or joins on the indexed columns. A B-tree index, the most common kind, keeps values in sorted order; the database can traverse it in logarithmic time and then follow pointers to the actual rows.

An index hurts when maintaining it costs more than it saves. Every insert, update, or delete that touches an indexed column must also update the index, so write-heavy workloads on heavily indexed tables slow down. Indexes also consume disk space and memory, and the query planner sometimes ignores an index if the table is small or if the query returns a large fraction of the rows, because reading the index and then the table is more work than a full scan.

Indexes hurt especially when they are unused or poorly chosen. A partial index with the wrong predicate, a multi-column index whose leading column is not in the query's filter, or an index on a column with very low cardinality can waste space and update cost while returning no benefit. Composite indexes are ordered by their leading column first, so a query that omits that column cannot use the index efficiently.

Covering indexes can help reads by including all columns the query needs, letting the database answer the query from the index alone; but they are wider, costlier to maintain, and more likely to be skipped by the planner for write-heavy patterns. The right index is one whose read benefit exceeds its write and storage cost for the actual workload.

TCP assigns each byte a sequence number. The sender numbers the data it transmits; the receiver uses those numbers to reassemble the stream in the right order.

The receiver acknowledges the next sequence number it expects. If segments arrive out of order, the receiver holds them in a buffer until the missing segment arrives. It sends duplicate acknowledgments for the gap, prompting the sender to retransmit.

The sender tracks which segments it has sent and which acknowledgments it has received. Unacknowledged data stays in a retransmission queue. A timeout or repeated duplicate acknowledgment triggers a resend.

The three-way handshake establishes the starting sequence numbers. Both sides pick an initial value, so every later byte has a unique, ordered identifier for that connection.

A mutex protects against race conditions in concurrent code by ensuring that only one thread or process enters a critical section at a time.

A race condition occurs when two or more threads read and write shared data in an order that produces incorrect results. The mutex wraps the code that touches the shared state. A thread must acquire the lock before entering and release it when leaving. If another thread already holds the lock, the caller waits.

The protected resource is not the mutex itself; it is the shared data or invariant the mutex guards. Common examples include a counter, a linked list, a file offset, or a buffer pool. Without the mutex, two threads could read the same value, both increment it, and both write back the same result, losing one update.

Mutexes do not prevent deadlocks automatically. If thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1, both block forever. Ordering lock acquisition prevents this.

They also do not protect against logical errors inside the critical section. A thread can still corrupt data if the code it runs under the lock is wrong. The mutex only enforces mutual exclusion; correctness inside the section remains the programmer's responsibility.

Garbage collection finds unused memory by tracing which objects the running program can still reach.

Most collectors start from a set of roots: local variables on thread stacks, static fields, and active registers. They mark every object reachable from those roots, then follow references inside those objects to mark more objects. Anything the mark phase never reaches is considered garbage.

The sweep phase then reclaims the unmarked objects. In a copying collector, live objects move to a new region and the old region is discarded whole. In a mark-sweep collector, the dead objects return to a free list.

Generational collectors exploit one observed fact: most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations and scan the young generation more often, since it produces the most garbage. Objects that survive several collections move to an older generation, which the collector scans less frequently.

A collector may pause all threads to mark the heap, or it may run concurrently while the program mutates objects. Concurrent collectors track changes the program makes during the trace, so they do not mistake a newly created reference for garbage.

The unused memory is therefore not memory the program no longer wants; it is memory the program can no longer name.

A race condition is a bug that appears when two threads or processes touch the same shared state in an order the programmer did not intend, and the result depends on which one wins the timing.

Picture two clerks updating the same ledger balance. Each reads the current amount, adds a deposit, and writes the new total back. Clerk A reads $100. Clerk B reads $100 before A finishes writing. A writes $120. B writes $130, having never seen A's deposit. One deposit vanishes.

The shared state is the ledger. The operations are read, compute, write. The bug is not in either clerk's arithmetic; it is in the interleaving. If A's read-modify-write runs to completion before B starts, the balance is correct. If they overlap, it is not.

Race conditions differ from deterministic bugs because the same code can pass tests and still fail in production. They require shared mutable state, non-atomic compound operations, and concurrent access without ordering. Remove any one of those and the race disappears.

The fix is usually to make the critical section exclusive: a mutex, an atomic compare-and-swap, or a design that gives each thread its own data. The tool depends on the shape of the shared work.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping copies of recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far enough away that fetching a value costs hundreds of clock cycles. The cache is smaller and faster, built from SRAM and placed on or near the core. When the CPU needs data, it checks the cache first. A hit returns the value in a few cycles. A miss sends the request to main memory and stalls the pipeline.

Programs exploit this through locality. Temporal locality means a value used once is likely to be used again soon. Spatial locality means nearby addresses are likely to be used next. The cache loads data in fixed-size lines, typically 64 bytes, so one fetch brings in the requested word and its neighbors.

Caches are organized in levels. L1 is smallest and fastest, often split into instruction and data caches. L2 and L3 are larger and slower but still beat main memory. A multi-core chip usually shares the last-level cache among cores.

The speedup is not automatic. A program that jumps randomly through a large array misses the cache repeatedly and performs nearly as poorly as if no cache existed. A program that walks memory sequentially reuses cache lines and runs many times faster.

Idempotency means the same HTTP request can be sent more than once without changing the result beyond the first time.

A `PUT` to `/users/42` with the same payload sets the user to the same state whether it is sent once or three times. A `DELETE` to `/users/42` removes the user on the first call; later calls find nothing and report the same outcome. The server does not add a second user, charge the card twice, or append duplicate records.

This matters because networks fail. A client may not receive a response and send the request again. An idempotent endpoint handles the retry safely. `GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` are idempotent by design. `POST` usually is not, because each call creates a new resource.

The practical test is simple: replay the request and compare the server state. If the second call leaves the system in the same shape as the first, the operation is idempotent.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a chain of name servers, each one more specific than the last.

The browser or operating system starts with a stub resolver. It checks its own cache first. If the address is not there, it sends a query to a recursive resolver, usually run by the ISP or a public service such as 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8.

The recursive resolver asks the root name servers. There are thirteen logical root servers, and they know only where the top-level domain servers live. The resolver asks a root server for `example.com`. The root server points it to the `.com` servers.

The resolver then asks a `.com` server. That server knows which name servers hold the records for `example.com`. It returns their addresses.

The resolver asks one of those authoritative name servers for `example.com`. That server holds the actual record, an A record for IPv4 or an AAAA record for IPv6, and returns the IP address.

The resolver hands the address back to the stub resolver, which caches it for the time specified by the record's TTL. The browser then opens a TCP connection to that address.

If any server along the chain has cached the answer, it returns it immediately and skips the rest of the walk. Caching is what keeps DNS fast.

A deadlock is a standoff between two or more threads, each holding a resource the others need and waiting for a resource the others hold.

Picture two trucks on a narrow bridge. Truck A owns the north half and waits for the south half. Truck B owns the south half and waits for the north half. Neither can move. Neither will back up. They stay there.

In code, thread 1 locks account A and asks for account B. Thread 2 locks account B and asks for account A. Both waits become permanent.

One way to avoid it is to order the locks. Every thread that needs both accounts takes A first, then B. Thread 2, wanting B, would have to take A first too. It blocks on A until thread 1 finishes, then proceeds. No circle forms.

The circle is the problem. Break the circle by removing one of its four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, or circular wait. Lock ordering attacks circular wait directly.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket chosen by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, that is a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions with chaining or open addressing.

Chaining keeps a linked list or tree inside each bucket. Every key that hashes to bucket *i* lives in bucket *i*'s chain. Lookup walks the chain and compares keys with `equals()` until it finds a match. Java's `HashMap` uses linked lists and switches to balanced trees when a chain grows past eight entries.

Open addressing places collisions in other buckets. Linear probing checks the next bucket, then the next, until it finds the key or an empty slot. Robin Hood hashing and quadratic probing are variations that reduce clustering or keep entries near their home bucket.

Load factor controls how often collisions occur. A hash map with more entries than buckets per entry rehashes: it allocates a larger array and redistributes every key. Rehashing keeps chains short and lookups near O(1) on average. In the worst case, every key collides and lookup becomes O(n).

A database index is a separate data structure that points to rows so the database can find them without reading every row in a table.

Most indexes are B-trees. The database keeps the indexed column values sorted in a tree of pages; each leaf page contains the value and a pointer to the matching row. To find rows where `email = 'x'`, the database walks the tree in O(log n) page reads instead of scanning the whole table.

Indexes speed up three things: lookups by exact value, range queries like `WHERE age BETWEEN 20 AND 30`, and joins that match columns across tables. They also let the database return results in sorted order without a separate sort step.

Indexes hurt in four common ways.

First, they take disk space. A copy of the indexed column plus row pointers lives alongside the table. On PostgreSQL, a single-column B-tree index is typically 10–30% of the table size; wide composite indexes can exceed the table.

Second, they slow down writes. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` that touches an indexed column must update the index too. On a write-heavy table, each additional index adds latency and contention. MySQL's InnoDB stores secondary indexes with primary-key lookups, so updating an indexed column can cost two index writes.

Third, they can make queries slower. If a query returns many rows, the database may decide to scan the table instead of bouncing between the index and the heap; this is especially true when the index is not selective, such as an index on a boolean column. A bad plan can also come from stale statistics or a query that the optimizer misprices.

Fourth, they add maintenance. Indexes fragment, their statistics drift, and they must be rebuilt or reanalyzed. PostgreSQL has autovacuum to keep statistics fresh; without it, plans degrade.

An index is worth it when the read savings outweigh these costs. A unique index on a primary key is almost always worth it. An index on a column that is rarely queried but frequently updated is usually not.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The receiver uses those numbers to reassemble the stream in the right order and to detect gaps.

Each TCP segment carries a sequence number for its first byte. The receiver acknowledges the next sequence number it expects. If segment 2 arrives before segment 1, the receiver holds segment 2 in a buffer and repeats the acknowledgment for segment 1 until segment 1 shows up. Once segment 1 arrives, TCP delivers both segments to the application in order.

The sender retransmits a segment if it does not get an acknowledgment within its retransmission timeout. That timeout adjusts based on measured round-trip times. Duplicate acknowledgments for the same sequence number also trigger a fast retransmit, since they usually mean a later segment arrived but an earlier one did not.

The receive window tells the sender how much buffer space remains at the receiver, so the sender does not overrun the buffer with out-of-order data.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions on shared data.

A race condition happens when two threads read and write the same memory at the same time, and the final value depends on the order their instructions run. A mutex prevents that by letting only one thread enter a critical section at a time.

When a thread wants to read or update shared state, it locks the mutex. If another thread already holds the lock, the caller waits. Once the owner unlocks the mutex, the next waiting thread enters. This serializes access, so updates happen one after another, not interleaved.

A mutex does not protect against bugs inside the critical section. If a thread modifies shared data incorrectly and then unlocks, the mutex has done its job: it let one thread in at a time. It also does not prevent deadlocks; two threads that each hold one mutex and wait for the other's will stall forever.

Common uses include guarding a counter, a shared queue, a connection pool, or a lazy-initialized singleton. In POSIX threads, `pthread_mutex_lock` and `pthread_mutex_unlock` mark the boundaries. In Rust, `std::sync::Mutex` wraps the data so the compiler only grants access while the lock is held.

The cost is contention: if many threads fight for the same mutex, they queue up and execution becomes serial. A coarse-grained mutex is simple but can become a bottleneck; a fine-grained design uses more locks on smaller pieces of data to reduce waiting.

Garbage collection finds unused memory by tracing which objects the running program can still reach.

Most collectors start from a set of roots: local variables on thread stacks, global variables, and CPU registers that hold references. They follow every reference from those roots to objects in the heap, then follow every reference inside those objects, and mark every object they visit. Any object the trace never reaches is unused, and the collector reclaims its memory.

Reference counting is a different approach. Each object stores a count of incoming references; when the count drops to zero, the object is unused. Reference counting cannot reclaim cycles: two objects that point only to each other keep each other alive even if nothing else points to them.

Generational collectors exploit the observation that most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations and scan the young generation more often, since it contains most of the garbage. Objects that survive several collections move to an older generation, which the collector scans less frequently.

A collector may run concurrently with the program or stop the world. Stop-the-world collectors pause all threads, trace the heap, and reclaim memory before resuming. Concurrent collectors reduce pause times but add complexity because the program keeps changing references while the collector works.

A race condition is a bug where the result of a program depends on the exact timing of two or more threads.

Consider two threads that each read a shared counter, add one, and write it back. Thread A reads 5. Before A writes 6, thread B reads 5 too. Both write 6. The counter should be 7, but it is 6 because the two increments overlapped.

The problem is the read-modify-write sequence. Each thread needs the whole sequence to run without interruption, but a mutex or atomic operation is missing, so the operating system scheduler interleaves them.

Race conditions are not limited to counters. They also corrupt linked lists when one thread inserts a node while another traverses it, or they produce duplicate primary keys when two processes check for an ID and then both insert it.

The fix is to make the critical section atomic: lock a mutex around the read and write, use an atomic increment, or rely on the database to enforce uniqueness.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far from the CPU on a separate chip, and a fetch takes dozens to hundreds of cycles. The cache is a smaller, faster memory on the same die. When the CPU reads an address, the hardware first checks the cache. A hit returns the data in a few cycles; a miss fetches a whole cache line from main memory and stores it nearby.

Programs tend to reuse data they just touched, and they often access nearby addresses next. Caches exploit both habits. Temporal locality means a second read of the same variable hits the cache. Spatial locality means reading one array element also loads its neighbors into the same cache line, so the next elements come from the cache.

Caches are arranged in levels. L1 is smallest and fastest, often split into separate instruction and data caches. L2 and L3 are larger and slower, shared across cores on most chips. A typical desktop CPU in 2024 has 32–64 KB of L1 per core, 256 KB–1 MB of L2, and 8–32 MB of shared L3.

The speedup is large when the working set fits in cache. A loop over an array that fits in L1 can run at near one element per cycle. The same loop on an array that exceeds RAM bandwidth stalls on memory fetches.

Caches also hurt when the access pattern fights them. False sharing happens when two cores write different variables that happen to live on the same cache line; the hardware keeps invalidating and reloading the line, and performance collapses. A cache miss on a cold read of a large structure can dominate runtime.

Idempotency means the same HTTP request can run more than once without changing the result beyond the first run.

A safe method is always idempotent: `GET` fetches a resource, and repeating it leaves the server the same. `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, and `TRACE` behave the same way.

Idempotency matters most for methods that change state. `PUT` replaces a resource with a specific version. Sending `PUT /users/42` with the same payload ten times ends with the same user as sending it once. `DELETE /users/42` removes the user; repeating it returns `404`, but the user stays gone.

`POST` is usually not idempotent. Each `POST /orders` creates a new order, so ten requests create ten orders. That is why payment endpoints and reservation systems often need extra guards, such as client-generated idempotency keys, to stop double charges or double bookings when a retry arrives.

A retry is the main reason APIs need idempotency. Networks drop replies, clients time out, and middleware resends. An idempotent endpoint handles the duplicate safely. A non-idempotent one may create duplicates, charge twice, or reserve the same seat again.

The HTTP spec lists `GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS`, and `TRACE` as idempotent by definition. `POST` and `PATCH` are not, though a particular `PATCH` implementation can be designed to be idempotent if it sets fields to absolute values rather than applying deltas.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a chain of name servers, each one closer to the answer.

When a browser or program needs `example.com`, it starts with a stub resolver on the local machine. That resolver usually asks a recursive resolver, often run by the ISP or a public service such as Cloudflare's `1.1.1.1` or Google's `8.8.8.8`.

The recursive resolver asks the root name servers. There are thirteen logical root servers, and they know where the top-level domains live. The root server replies with the addresses of the `.com` name servers.

The resolver then asks a `.com` server. It replies with the addresses of the name servers for `example.com`.

Finally, the resolver asks one of those name servers. It returns the IP address for `example.com`, perhaps `93.184.216.34`.

The resolver caches each answer. The next query for `example.com` uses the cached address until the record's time-to-live expires. Caching is why DNS changes can take minutes or hours to reach everyone.

Each step uses UDP on port 53 for ordinary queries, though DNS over HTTPS and DNS over TLS now encrypt requests between the stub and the recursive resolver.

A deadlock is a standoff between two or more threads, each holding a resource the other needs and waiting for the other to release it first.

Picture two bank accounts and two threads. Thread A locks account 1 and asks for account 2. Thread B locks account 2 and asks for account 1. Neither can finish. Both wait forever unless something breaks the cycle.

One way to avoid it is lock ordering. Every thread acquires locks in the same global order. If both threads must lock account 1 before account 2, the second thread waits for account 1, but it never holds account 2 while doing so. The cycle cannot form.

Other methods exist. Timeouts let a thread abandon a lock attempt and retry. Resource hierarchy assigns each resource a rank and forbids acquiring a lower-ranked lock while holding a higher-ranked one. Deadlock detection watches the wait graph and kills a thread to break the cycle.

Lock ordering is the simplest when the set of locks is known in advance. It turns a potential cycle into a queue.

Most hash maps resolve collisions with chaining or open addressing.

Chaining keeps a linked list or tree inside each bucket. Every key that hashes to bucket *i* lives in bucket *i*'s chain. Lookup walks the chain and compares keys with `equals()` until it finds a match. Java's `HashMap` uses linked lists and switches to balanced trees when a chain grows past eight entries.

Open addressing places collisions in other buckets. Linear probing checks the next bucket, then the next, until it finds the key or an empty slot. Robin Hood hashing and quadratic probing are variations that reduce clustering or keep entries near their home bucket.

Load factor controls how often collisions occur. A hash map with more entries than buckets per entry rehashes: it allocates a larger array and redistributes every key. Rehashing keeps chains short and lookups near O(1) on average. In the worst case, every key collides and lookup becomes O(n).

I need to acknowledge the request and then answer it. The user wants an explanation of how TCP keeps data in order, with specific style constraints: E. B. White / George Orwell plain register, every sentence a fact, active voice, concrete nouns, short words, no preamble/summary/meta-narration.

TCP sequence numbers label every byte sent. The sender increments the sequence number by the number of bytes in each segment. The receiver uses these numbers to reassemble segments in the right order, even if the network delivers them out of sequence.

The receiver acknowledges the next byte it expects. It buffers out-of-order segments and waits for the missing byte to arrive. Once the gap fills, it delivers the contiguous stream to the application.

The sender retransmits a segment if the acknowledgment does not arrive within the retransmission timeout. Duplicate acknowledgments trigger faster retransmission before the timeout expires.

The sliding window lets the sender have multiple unacknowledged segments in flight. Sequence numbers and window bounds keep the receiver from accepting old or duplicate segments after a connection recovers from a delay.

A mutex protects against concurrent threads or processes entering a critical section at the same time.

A critical section is a region of code that reads or writes shared state. If two threads execute that region together, one can overwrite the other's work, read a half-updated structure, or leave invariants broken.

The mutex enforces mutual exclusion. One thread locks the mutex before entering the section. Other threads that call `lock()` block until the owner calls `unlock()`. Only one thread runs the critical section at a time.

This prevents race conditions on shared data. It does not prevent deadlocks; two threads can still block forever if each holds one mutex and waits for the other's.

A garbage collector finds unused memory by tracing reachable objects from a set of roots.

The roots are the starting points the runtime already knows about: local variables on thread stacks, global variables, CPU registers, and handles held by the language runtime. Any object the program can still use must be reachable from at least one root.

The collector follows references. If a root points to object A, and A points to object B, both A and B are reachable. The collector walks this graph, marking every object it visits.

Objects the walk never reaches are unreachable. The program has no path to read or write them, so the collector reclaims their memory.

Some collectors add a reference count to each object. The count tracks how many references point to the object. When the count drops to zero, the object is unreachable and the collector frees it immediately. Reference counting alone cannot collect cycles; two objects that point only to each other keep their counts above zero even when nothing else references them.

Generational collectors exploit the observation that most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations and trace the young generation more often than the old one. A few old objects that point to young objects are recorded separately so the collector does not have to scan the entire old generation every cycle.

A race condition happens when two threads access the same memory and the result depends on the order of their operations.

Imagine two threads incrementing a shared counter. Each thread reads the counter, adds one, and writes it back. Thread A reads 5. Before A writes 6, thread B reads 5. Both threads write 6. The counter should be 7, but it is 6 because the two updates overlapped.

The problem is the read-modify-write sequence. The operating system can interrupt a thread between any two instructions. When the sequence is not atomic, another thread can slip into the gap and operate on stale data.

Locks prevent this. One thread acquires the lock, reads, adds one, writes, and releases the lock. The other thread waits. The counter increments by two, as it should.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits on separate chips, and fetching from it takes hundreds of clock cycles. The cache is smaller memory built into the same chip as the CPU. A load that hits the cache completes in a few cycles instead of hundreds.

Programs tend to reuse the same data and instructions soon after using them. The cache exploits this by storing copies of recently accessed memory locations. It also fetches neighboring bytes together in blocks called cache lines, so a single miss often brings in the next values the program will need.

When the CPU needs to read or write, it checks the cache first. If the data is there, it uses the cached copy. If not, it fetches the block from main memory and stores a copy in the cache. Writes either update the cache and memory together or mark the cache line dirty and flush it later.

A cache miss still costs the full main-memory latency. Programs that jump through memory randomly miss often. Programs that scan arrays or reuse small working sets hit often and run faster.

Idempotency means an HTTP request produces the same server state no matter how many times the client sends it.

A `PUT` request to `/users/42` with the same body sets the same name, email, and preferences each time. The first request creates or updates the record. The second, third, and tenth identical requests leave the record in the same state. The client can retry after a timeout without fear of creating ten copies.

A `POST` to `/charges` is not idempotent by default. Retry a failed charge request and the server may run the card twice. APIs make such calls idempotent by having the client send a unique key, such as `Idempotency-Key: abc-123`. The server stores the key with the result. A retry with the same key returns the stored result instead of running the charge again.

Safe methods such as `GET`, `HEAD`, and `OPTIONS` are also idempotent because they do not change state. Calling them repeatedly reads the same resource, though the value may change between calls from other traffic.

Idempotency does not guarantee the same response every time. It guarantees the same effect. A `DELETE` to `/users/42` returns `204` the first time and `404` the second, but the user stays deleted.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a hierarchy of servers.

A browser or application first asks a recursive resolver, usually run by the operating system or an ISP. The resolver checks its cache. If it has no answer, it starts at the root.

The root server does not know the address. It points the resolver to the server for the top-level domain, such as `.com` or `.org`. The top-level server points to the authoritative server for the specific domain, such as `example.com`.

The authoritative server holds the record. It returns the IP address for the name. The resolver sends that address back to the application and keeps a cached copy for the time specified by the record's TTL.

If the name has a CNAME record, the resolver follows the alias and looks up the canonical name. If the record is an A record, it returns an IPv4 address. If it is an AAAA record, it returns an IPv6 address.

Each step uses UDP on port 53 by default. Large responses or zone transfers use TCP.

A deadlock is a standoff between two or more threads where each one waits for another to release a resource.

Picture two threads and two locks. Thread A locks the account file. Thread B locks the log file. Thread A then tries to lock the log file, but B already holds it, so A waits. Thread B tries to lock the account file, but A already holds it, so B waits. Neither can proceed. Neither will release what it already holds.

One way to avoid this is to lock resources in a fixed order. Every thread that needs both files locks the account file first and the log file second. If B reaches the log file first, it must wait for the account file. It cannot hold the log file while waiting for the account file, so the circular wait cannot form.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket chosen by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, that is a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions with chaining or open addressing.

Chaining keeps a linked list or tree inside each bucket. Every key that hashes to bucket *i* lives in bucket *i*'s chain. Lookup walks the chain and compares keys with `equals()` until it finds a match. Java's `HashMap` uses linked lists and switches to balanced trees when a chain grows past eight entries.

Open addressing places collisions in other buckets. Linear probing checks the next bucket, then the next, until it finds the key or an empty slot. Robin Hood hashing and quadratic probing are variations that reduce clustering or keep entries near their home bucket.

Load factor controls how often collisions occur. A hash map with more entries than buckets per entry rehashes: it allocates a larger array and redistributes every key. Rehashing keeps chains short and lookups near O(1) on average. In the worst case, every key collides and lookup becomes O(n).

A database index is a separate data structure that points to rows in a table, built on one or more columns so the database can find values without scanning every row.

The most common index is a B-tree. It stores column values in sorted pages, with parent pages holding ranges that guide the search downward. A lookup on an indexed column starts at the root, follows the range pointers, and reaches the leaf that contains the matching value or values. From there the database reads the row IDs or row pointers and fetches the actual rows.

Indexes help when the query filters, sorts, or joins on the indexed column. A `WHERE` clause on an indexed column can turn a full-table scan into a few page reads. A join between two large tables on an indexed foreign key avoids nested loops over unsorted heaps. Sorting on an indexed column can skip an explicit sort step because the index already returns values in order.

Indexes hurt in several concrete ways.

They consume disk space. Every index is a copy of part of the data, plus tree structure. A table with six secondary indexes may store several times the table's raw size in indexes.

They slow writes. On every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE`, the database must update not only the table but every index that covers the changed columns. A write-heavy table with many indexes spends much of its time maintaining trees rather than storing rows.

They can make queries slower. If a query returns many rows or uses a low-selectivity predicate, the database may spend more time jumping between the index and the table than it would scanning sequentially. This is especially true for queries that fetch most of the table, where an index lookup becomes random I/O across many pages instead of a sequential scan.

They add lock contention and maintenance cost. Rebuilding or rebalancing a large index takes time and I/O. Some databases lock the table or partition during index creation. Query planners can also choose the wrong index, or choose an index when a sequential scan would be cheaper, producing slow plans that are hard to diagnose without reading the execution plan.

So an index is a trade: faster reads on specific columns against slower writes, more storage, and the risk of bad plans when the query does not match the index well.

TCP assigns each byte a sequence number. The sender numbers the bytes it transmits, and the receiver uses those numbers to reassemble the stream in the right order.

The receiver acknowledges the highest contiguous sequence number it has received. If a segment arrives out of order, the receiver holds it in a buffer and waits for the missing segment to fill the gap. It does not deliver the later data to the application until the gap closes.

The sender detects a missing segment when it does not get an acknowledgment within its retransmission timeout, or when it receives three duplicate acknowledgments for the same sequence number. It then retransmits the missing segment.

Sequence numbers also let TCP discard duplicate segments. If a segment arrives with a sequence number the receiver has already processed, TCP drops it.

This mechanism keeps the byte stream ordered end-to-end, even when the network delivers packets out of sequence, drops them, or duplicates them.

A mutex protects a program against races on shared data when many threads use it at once.

A race happens when two threads read, modify, and write the same memory without ordering. Thread A reads a counter as five, thread B reads it as five, both add one, both write six. The counter should be seven; it is six.

A mutex is a lock. One thread acquires it before touching the shared data. The operating system or runtime lets only one thread hold the mutex at a time. Other threads that try to acquire it wait until the holder releases it.

This serializes access. The counter update becomes: thread A reads five, adds one, writes six, releases the lock; thread B then reads six, adds one, writes seven. No update is lost.

A mutex does not protect against all concurrency bugs. It does not prevent deadlocks if threads acquire locks in inconsistent orders. It does not prevent a thread from forgetting to lock before accessing the data. It only guarantees that the locked region runs by one thread at a time.

A garbage collector finds unused memory by tracing which objects the program can still reach.

Most collectors start from a set of roots: local variables on thread stacks, static fields, and handles held by the runtime. They follow references from each root to the objects it points to, then follow references inside those objects, and so on. Every object reached this way is marked live.

Objects the trace never reaches are unused. The collector reclaims their memory. In a mark-sweep collector, the mark phase walks the graph and the sweep phase frees unmarked objects. In a copying collector, live objects are copied to a new region and the old region is discarded whole. In a generational collector, the heap is split by age; young generations are collected more often because most objects die young, and objects that survive several collections are promoted to an older generation.

Reference counting is a different approach. Each object stores a count of incoming references. When the count drops to zero, the object is unused and can be freed immediately. Reference counting cannot collect cycles: if object A points to B and B points to A, both counts stay above zero even when nothing else references them. A tracing collector can reclaim such cycles because the cycle is not reachable from any root.

The collector does not know whether the program will use an object in the future; it only knows whether the object is reachable now. An object the program has forgotten but that is still referenced by a live object will not be reclaimed.

A race condition is a bug where a program's result depends on the timing or order of operations that run at the same time.

Consider two threads that increment the same counter. Each thread does three things: read the counter, add one, and write it back. Thread A reads 5. Before A writes, thread B reads 5 too. A writes 6. B writes 6. The counter ends at 6, though two increments ran.

The bug is not that the threads ran wrong code. Each thread ran its own steps correctly. The bug is the interleaving: the second read happened before the first write, so one update was lost.

Race conditions appear where shared state meets concurrent access and at least one access changes the state. They do not require many threads; two threads and one shared variable are enough. They also do not always fail: if A finishes before B starts, the counter reaches 7. That intermittent failure makes races hard to find and reproduce.

The fix is to make the read-add-write sequence atomic, usually with a lock or an atomic increment instruction. Then the second thread cannot read the counter until the first thread has written it back.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far from the CPU on a separate chip. Fetching from it takes hundreds of clock cycles. The cache is smaller memory made from faster transistors, placed on the same die as the core. A load that hits the cache completes in a few cycles instead of hundreds.

Programs access memory with locality. They reuse the same variables soon after touching them, and they read adjacent addresses in sequence. The cache exploits this by copying whole blocks, called cache lines, typically 64 bytes each. When the program reads one byte, the cache brings in the surrounding bytes too.

Caches are layered. A modern CPU has a small L1 cache per core, a larger L2 cache, and a shared L3 cache. L1 is fastest but holds only tens of kilobytes. L3 is slower but holds many megabytes. The hardware checks L1 first, then L2, then L3, then main memory.

A cache hit avoids the slow trip to RAM. A cache miss stalls the pipeline while the hardware fetches the line. Programs that stride through memory unpredictably miss often. Programs that reuse small working sets hit often and run much faster.

Idempotency means the same HTTP request can be sent more than once without changing the result beyond the first time.

A `PUT` to `/users/42` with the same payload sets the user to the same values whether it runs once or ten times. A `DELETE` to `/users/42` removes the user on the first call and leaves nothing to remove on the second; repeating it does not delete anything extra.

This matters because networks fail. A client may not receive a response and send the request again. If the endpoint is idempotent, the retry is safe. If it is not, a duplicate `POST` to `/orders` might create two orders.

Safe methods such as `GET` and `HEAD` are idempotent by nature: they do not change state. `PUT`, `DELETE`, and some `POST` operations can be made idempotent by giving the client a unique key or by checking the current state before acting.

The server still processes each request; idempotency is a property of the effect, not of whether work happens. A duplicate call may return the same response, update nothing new, or report that the resource is already gone.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a hierarchy of servers, each one narrowing the search.

A computer starts with a resolver, usually run by the operating system or the local network. The resolver first checks its own cache. If the name is there, it returns the address immediately.

If the cache misses, the resolver asks a recursive resolver, often provided by an ISP or a public service such as 8.8.8.8. That resolver does the walking.

The walk begins at a root server. There are thirteen logical root servers, and their addresses are baked into every resolver. The root server does not know the final address. It points the resolver to the top-level domain server for the suffix, such as `.com` or `.org`.

The resolver asks that TLD server. The TLD server does not know the final address either. It points the resolver to the authoritative server for the specific domain, such as `example.com`.

The resolver asks the authoritative server. That server holds the record that maps the name to an address. It returns the A record for IPv4 or the AAAA record for IPv6.

The resolver hands the address back to the computer, caches it for the time specified in the record's TTL, and the computer opens a connection.

If any server along the chain fails to answer, the resolver retries or tries another server. If the authoritative server says the name does not exist, the resolver returns an error, and the lookup fails.

A deadlock is a standoff between threads or processes that each hold a resource the other needs.

Thread A locks the user database. Thread B locks the order database. Thread A then asks for the order lock, but Thread B already holds it. Thread B asks for the user lock, but Thread A already holds it. Both wait forever. Neither releases its lock because neither can proceed.

One way to avoid this is to make every thread acquire locks in the same order. If both threads always lock the user database before the order database, the second thread cannot hold the order lock while waiting for the user lock. The first thread finishes both locks and releases them; the second thread follows. No cycle forms, so no deadlock.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket chosen by running the key through a hash function and reducing that hash to an index within the array of buckets. Two different keys can produce the same index; that event is a collision.

The two common responses to a collision are chaining and open addressing. Chaining keeps a linked list, tree, or other structure at each bucket. Every entry that hashes to the same index goes into that structure. Open addressing places the entry in another bucket within the same array, found by probing forward until an empty slot appears.

Load factor governs performance. As the ratio of stored entries to bucket count rises, collisions become more frequent. Most implementations resize the backing array and rehash every entry into the larger array once the load factor crosses a threshold, often around 0.75.

The hash function itself matters. A poor hash function clusters keys into a few buckets and defeats the array. A good one spreads keys evenly across the whole range. Many maps also mix the hash bits before reducing them, so that high-order bits influence low-order indices and break patterns in the key distribution.

A database index is a separate structure that points to rows so the database can find them without reading every page.

Most indexes are B-trees. Each leaf holds a key value and a pointer to the row's location on disk. To find a row by an indexed column, the database walks the tree in O(log n) page reads instead of scanning the whole table.

An index hurts when maintaining it costs more than it saves. Every insert, update, or delete that touches an indexed column must also update the index, often by splitting B-tree pages and writing extra WAL entries. A table with six indexes can turn a simple write into six tree traversals plus lock acquisitions.

It also hurts when the query does not use it. A low-cardinality column—say, a boolean flag on a million-row table—may return half the rows anyway, so the optimizer ignores the index and scans. If it does use the index, it may bounce between the index leaves and the heap for many rows, which is slower than a sequential scan.

Indexes consume disk and memory. Each index is a copy of part of the table, sized by the column width and row count. Unused indexes still occupy cache and slow backups and replication.

Finally, an index hurts when it is the wrong shape for the query. A single-column index on `last_name` cannot help a query that filters by `last_name` and `first_name` unless the database can do an index intersection, which many cannot. A composite index on `(last_name, first_name)` would serve that query, but it would not help a query filtering only by `first_name` because the leading column is wrong.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. Each segment carries a sequence number that marks where its data belongs in the stream.

The receiver acknowledges the next byte it expects. If segment 1000 arrives but 500 is still missing, the receiver keeps asking for 500 and buffers 1000 until the gap closes.

The sender keeps a window of unacknowledged bytes. It retransmits anything the receiver does not acknowledge within a timeout, and it slides the window forward only when fresh acknowledgments arrive.

This sequence-and-acknowledge loop, plus buffering at both ends, lets TCP deliver bytes to the application in the exact order they were sent, even when the network delivers segments out of order, drops some, or duplicates others.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions on shared data.

A race condition happens when two threads touch the same memory at the same time and at least one thread writes. Without a mutex, a read can see a half-written value, two writes can overwrite each other, or an update can use a stale value.

A mutex enforces mutual exclusion. Only one thread can hold the lock at a time. That thread must release the lock before another can enter the protected section.

The protected section is called the critical section. It should be as small as possible, because while one thread holds the mutex, every other thread that wants the same lock waits.

A mutex does not protect against every concurrency problem. It does not prevent deadlocks, where two threads each hold a lock the other wants. It does not prevent priority inversion, where a low-priority thread holds a lock a high-priority thread needs. It also does not make a shared resource safe if threads access it through a path the mutex does not cover.

Used correctly, a mutex turns concurrent access into serialized access for the guarded data. That is its only job.

Garbage collection finds unused memory by tracing what the running program can still reach.

The collector starts from a set of roots: local variables on thread stacks, global variables, and CPU registers that hold references. It marks every object those roots point to, then every object those objects point to, and so on, until it runs out of reachable references.

Any object the trace never reached is unused. The collector sweeps those objects and reclaims their memory.

Some collectors add a reference count to each object. When the count drops to zero, the object is unreachable and can be reclaimed immediately. Reference counting alone cannot catch cycles—two objects that point to each other but are otherwise unreachable—so most systems combine it with tracing or use tracing alone.

Generational collectors exploit a pattern: most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations, scan the young generation often, and scan older objects only when enough new garbage has accumulated. This reduces the work per collection.

A tracing collector must pause the program or coordinate with it so that references do not move while the trace is in progress. The pause length, the coordination cost, and the frequency of collection determine whether the collector helps or hurts a given program.

A race condition is a bug that appears when two threads read and write the same data at the same time, and the final result depends on the exact moment each thread runs.

Picture two cashiers updating the same ledger. The ledger says 100. Cashier A reads 100, adds 10, and writes 110. Cashier B reads 100, adds 20, and writes 120. If B reads before A finishes, B writes 120 and A's 110 overwrites it. The bank expected 130; it got 120.

The same thing happens in code. Thread A reads a counter, increments it, and writes it back. Thread B does the same. If the operating system pauses A after the read, B can run the whole increment and write before A resumes. One increment disappears.

A race condition is not the same as two threads doing unrelated work at once. It requires shared state and at least one write. Reads alone do not corrupt data; a read during a write can.

The fix is usually a lock, an atomic operation, or a design that keeps the data in one thread. The root cause is always the same: the program assumes a sequence that the scheduler does not guarantee.

A CPU cache speeds a program by keeping recently used memory close to the core.

A modern CPU runs at gigahertz. Main memory answers in tens to hundreds of nanoseconds. That gap is long enough for the core to execute hundreds of instructions while waiting. The cache sits between them, built from faster SRAM, and holds copies of memory the program has touched.

Caches work because programs reuse data. Temporal locality means a byte accessed once is likely accessed again soon. Spatial locality means a byte near an accessed one is likely next. The cache exploits both: it stores whole lines, typically 64 bytes, and keeps recently loaded lines ready.

When the core asks for data, the cache checks first. A hit returns in a few cycles. A miss sends the request to main memory and stalls the pipeline. A program with good locality hits often; one that jumps through memory randomly misses often.

Caches are arranged in levels. L1 is smallest and fastest, often split into instruction and data caches. L2 and L3 are larger and slower but still faster than RAM. A core usually has private L1 and L2; L3 is shared across cores.

False sharing is one way caches hurt. Two cores write different variables that happen to live on the same cache line. Each write invalidates the other's copy, forcing both to refetch from memory. The program runs slower even though the cores touch unrelated data.

Cache size and layout are fixed. A program cannot grow the cache, but it can arrange its work so that each load brings useful bytes and so that repeated work touches the same bytes again.

Idempotency means an HTTP request can be sent more than once without changing the result beyond the first time.

A client might retry a `PUT /users/42` because the network dropped before the response arrived. If the request is idempotent, the server ends up with the same user data whether the request arrived once or three times. The second and third requests do not create extra users or corrupt the record.

Safe methods are idempotent by definition. `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, and `TRACE` should not change server state at all, so repeating them is harmless.

`PUT` and `DELETE` are meant to be idempotent but are not safe. `PUT /users/42` with the same body should overwrite the resource with identical data each time. `DELETE /users/42` should remove the resource and return the same status on later calls, usually `404` once it is gone.

`POST` is usually not idempotent. Each `POST /orders` typically creates a new order. A retry without safeguards can produce duplicates.

Implementing idempotency for `POST` often requires an idempotency key. The client generates a unique key, such as a UUID, and sends it in a header. The server stores the key with the response and returns the stored response for repeats. Stripe's `Idempotency-Key` header works this way.

Idempotency does not mean a request has no side effects. `DELETE` clearly has side effects. It means the side effects of repeated identical requests match the side effects of a single request.

Networks are unreliable. Timeouts, retries, and middleware redeliveries happen. Idempotency lets the client retry without asking the server what happened first.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a chain of name servers.

When a browser or program needs `example.com`, it first asks a recursive resolver. The resolver checks its cache. If it has no answer, it starts at the root.

The root name servers know the addresses of the top-level domain servers. The resolver asks a root server where to find `.com`. The root server returns the addresses of the `.com` servers.

The resolver then asks a `.com` server about `example.com`. That server knows the authoritative name servers for `example.com` and returns their addresses.

Finally, the resolver asks one of those authoritative servers. That server holds the record that maps `example.com` to an IP address, such as `93.184.216.34`. It returns the record.

The resolver caches the answer at each level and hands the address back to the browser. The browser opens a TCP connection to that address.

Each step uses UDP or TCP on port 53. The whole chain usually finishes in milliseconds because most answers are already cached.

A deadlock is a standoff between threads or processes where each one waits for a resource another holds, and none can move.

Picture two clerks and two forms. Clerk A picks up Form 1 and will not release it until he gets Form 2. Clerk B picks up Form 2 and will not release it until he gets Form 1. Both sit still forever.

In code, the resources are usually locks. Thread A locks `account_x`, then tries to lock `account_y`. Thread B locks `account_y`, then tries to lock `account_x`. If their timing overlaps, each holds one lock and waits for the other. The program freezes.

Four conditions must all hold for a deadlock: mutual exclusion (only one thread can hold a resource), hold-and-wait (a thread holds one resource while asking for another), no preemption (resources cannot be taken away), and circular wait (the waiting forms a loop).

One way to avoid it is lock ordering. Every thread must acquire locks in the same global order. If both threads always lock `account_x` before `account_y`, the second thread cannot hold `account_y` while waiting for `account_x`. The circular wait disappears.

Lock ordering costs discipline. Programmers must know the order, and the order must stay stable as the code changes. But it is a direct fix: it breaks one of the four necessary conditions, so the deadlock cannot form.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket numbered by the key's hash code. Two keys can land in the same bucket; that is a collision.

Separate chaining hangs a linked list from the bucket. Each new colliding key appends to the list. Lookup walks the list and compares keys with `equals()`.

Open addressing places the colliding key in the next empty bucket, often by probing forward. Linear probing checks the next slot; quadratic probing jumps by increasing squares; double hashing uses a second hash to pick the step size.

Load factor governs performance. Chaining slows as lists lengthen; open addressing clusters and degrades. Resizing to more buckets and rehashing every entry restores the ratio.

The choice trades memory against probes. Chaining tolerates high load; open addressing avoids pointer overhead but needs sparse tables.

A database index is a separate data structure that points to rows so the engine can find them without scanning the whole table.

Most indexes are B-trees. They store the indexed column values in sorted order, with leaf nodes holding row identifiers or pointers to the actual data. A lookup on an indexed column walks the tree in O(log n) time instead of reading every row.

An index hurts when maintaining it costs more than it saves. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` on the indexed column must also update the index, so write-heavy tables with many indexes slow down. Indexes also consume disk space and memory; wide or redundant indexes waste both.

An index fails to help when the query does not match it. A query with a leading wildcard, a function on the column, or a low-cardinality column may still scan the table. The query planner can ignore an index if it estimates that a full scan is cheaper, especially on small tables where the index lookup overhead exceeds the benefit.

Covering indexes help reads because the index alone satisfies the query. Composite indexes help only when the query uses a leftmost prefix of the columns. Partial indexes help when the query filters on a common subset. Each of these is a trade-off: faster reads, slower writes, more storage.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The sender puts a sequence number on each segment; the receiver uses that number to reassemble the stream in the right order.

The receiver acknowledges the next byte it expects. If a segment arrives out of order, the receiver holds it in a buffer and sends a duplicate acknowledgment for the missing byte. The sender retransmits when it does not get an acknowledgment in time.

This sequence-and-acknowledgment loop also detects loss. A missing segment leaves a gap in the byte stream, so the receiver keeps asking for the lost number until it arrives.

A mutex protects a program against races on shared data.

When two threads touch the same variable at once, one can overwrite the other mid-step. A mutex makes those threads take turns. A thread locks the mutex before entering the critical section, does its work, then unlocks it. Only one thread holds the lock at a time; the rest wait.

Without it, updates can interleave. One thread reads a value, another writes it, and the first writes back a stale result. A mutex prevents that by serializing access to the guarded region.

It does not prevent deadlocks on its own. If thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1, both stall. Ordering locks consistently fixes that.

It also does not stop bugs inside the critical section. It only keeps other threads out while one thread runs it.

A garbage collector finds unused memory by tracing what the program can still reach.

It starts from roots: local variables on thread stacks, global variables, and CPU registers that hold references. Anything reachable directly or through references from those roots is alive.

The collector walks the object graph. If object A points to object B, B is reachable. It marks each reachable object. Objects the walk never touches stay unmarked.

After marking, the collector sweeps. It treats unmarked objects as garbage and reclaims their memory. Some collectors also compact the live objects to remove gaps.

Reference counting is a different approach. Each object stores a count of incoming references. When the count hits zero, the object is unused. It reclaims memory immediately but cannot clean up cycles: two objects that point only to each other keep each other's count above zero.

Generational collectors exploit a pattern: most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations and scan the young generation more often, which reduces work.

A race condition is a bug where the result of a program depends on the exact timing of independent threads.

Two threads read and write the same variable without coordination. Thread A reads a counter value of 3. Before A can write back 4, thread B also reads 3 and writes back 4. The counter should be 5, but it ends up at 4 because the two updates overlapped.

The bug is not in either thread alone. It appears only when their operations interleave in a particular order. Reordering instructions, cache delays, or scheduler timing can make the failure intermittent, which is why race conditions are hard to reproduce.

The fix is to make the read-increment-write sequence atomic. A mutex, an atomic increment, or a compare-and-swap loop prevents the second thread from entering the critical section while the first thread is still inside.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping copies of recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far from the cores. Fetching from it costs hundreds of clock cycles. The cache is smaller and faster, made of SRAM, and lives on the same chip. When the CPU needs a value, it checks the cache first. A hit returns the data in a few cycles. A miss sends the request to main memory and stalls the pipeline.

Caches exploit locality. Temporal locality means a byte used once is likely to be used again soon. Spatial locality means nearby bytes are likely to be used next. The cache fetches an entire cache line, typically 64 bytes, so one miss brings in a whole neighborhood of data.

A multi-level hierarchy separates size from speed. L1 is smallest and fastest, often split into instruction and data caches. L2 is larger and slower. L3 is shared across cores and bigger still. The CPU searches L1, then L2, then L3, then RAM.

Cache misses cost more than the saved cycles suggest. A miss can evict useful data, trigger coherency traffic between cores, or saturate the memory bus. Programs that jump through memory randomly miss often. Programs that walk arrays sequentially hit often.

Idempotency means an HTTP request produces the same outcome no matter how many times the client sends it.

A safe, idempotent method is GET. Calling GET /orders/42 once returns the same order as calling it ten times. The server does not change state.

PUT is idempotent but not safe. Sending PUT /users/42 with the same payload the first time updates the record; sending it again leaves the record in the same final state. Repeating the request does not apply the change twice.

POST is usually not idempotent. POST /charges with the same card details can create two charges. The client must add a unique idempotency key, such as Idempotency-Key: abc-123, if it wants the server to recognize a retry and return the first result instead of running the operation again.

The guarantee matters when networks fail. A client may retry a request that actually reached the server. Without idempotency, the retry creates duplicate work. With it, the server can detect the duplicate and return the existing response.

Idempotency is about effect, not just return value. A request can return a different status code on retry—201 the first time, 200 the second—and still be idempotent, as long as the server's state ends up the same.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a hierarchy of servers.

A browser or app first checks its own cache. If the name is not there, it asks a recursive resolver, usually run by the operating system or the ISP. The resolver does the legwork.

The resolver starts at a root server. The root does not know the address, but it points to the server for the top-level domain, such as `.com` or `.org`. The resolver asks that TLD server. The TLD server points to the authoritative server for the specific domain, such as `example.com`. The resolver asks that server, which returns the IP address.

Each answer has a time-to-live value. The resolver caches the result for that many seconds and returns it to the browser.

If the authoritative server holds a CNAME record, it sends an alias instead of an address. The resolver then looks up the canonical name and follows the chain.

The whole exchange usually finishes in milliseconds, but a stale cache or a missing record can make a name fail to resolve.

A deadlock is a standoff between threads or processes that each hold a resource the other needs.

Thread A locks the account-balance mutex and then tries to lock the transaction-log mutex. Thread B already holds the transaction-log mutex and is waiting for the account-balance mutex. Neither releases what it has, so neither can finish.

One fix is to lock resources in the same order everywhere. If every thread always takes the account-balance mutex before the transaction-log mutex, the circular wait cannot form. A thread that wants the second mutex will wait, but it will not hold the first mutex while doing so.

A hash map stores each key-value pair at an index produced by a hash function. When two keys hash to the same index, the map has a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions by chaining or open addressing. Chaining keeps a linked list or tree at each bucket; every entry that hashes to the bucket goes into that list. Open addressing probes for the next empty slot, using a fixed sequence such as linear, quadratic, or double hashing.

Chaining keeps the table simple but uses extra memory for pointers. Open addressing avoids pointers but clusters entries and can degrade if the load factor grows too high. A well-implemented hash map rehashes into a larger table when the load factor crosses a threshold, usually around 0.75, to keep both chains and probe sequences short.

The worst case—every key collides—turns lookup into a linear scan, O(n). A good hash function and resizing make the average case O(1).

An index helps when the query filters, joins, or orders on the indexed column. It also helps when the database can answer the query from the index alone, without touching the table. It hurts when it does not match the query: the database still scans the table, and now it has spent time checking an irrelevant tree.

An index hurts on writes. Every insert, update, or delete that touches the indexed column must update the tree, often splitting pages and writing extra log records. A table with many indexes pays this cost many times per row change.

An index hurts when it is unused but maintained. It consumes disk space and memory, and it slows every write without speeding any read. The database may also choose a bad plan: if the optimizer misestimates the number of matching rows, it may scan the index and then fetch most of the table, which is slower than a plain table scan.

An index hurts when the data is small. On a table that fits in memory, a sequential scan can be faster than bouncing through tree pages.

Indexes help selective queries on large tables. They hurt when they are redundant, unused, over-applied to write-heavy tables, or chosen by an optimizer that guessed wrong.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The receiver uses those numbers to put the bytes back in order and to spot gaps.

Each TCP segment carries a sequence number. That number marks the first byte in the segment. The receiver acknowledges the next byte it expects, not the last one it got. If segment 2 arrives before segment 1, the receiver holds segment 2 in a buffer and repeats the acknowledgment for byte 1 until segment 1 shows up.

The sender keeps every sent segment in a retransmission queue until the receiver acknowledges it. If an acknowledgment does not arrive before the retransmission timeout expires, the sender sends the segment again.
