A good hash function matters more than the collision strategy. A weak function clusters keys into a few buckets and turns every lookup into a linear scan, no matter how clever the table.

A database index is a separate, smaller structure that points to rows so the engine can find them without scanning the whole table.

Most indexes are B-trees. The database keeps the indexed column values sorted in a tree of pages; a lookup walks from the root to a leaf, then follows a pointer to the row. A binary search on a sorted list would need roughly log₂(n) comparisons; a B-tree needs roughly log₁₀₀(n) page reads because each page holds many keys. On a million-row table that is about three page reads instead of twenty.

An index helps when the query filters, joins, or sorts on the indexed column. It also helps when the query can be answered from the index alone, without touching the table. But an index costs space and slows writes. Every insert, update, or delete that touches an indexed column must update the index too, and that update may split or merge B-tree pages.

An index hurts when the query returns many rows. If a query asks for every customer in California and half the table qualifies, the database may read half the index and half the table. A full table scan can be faster because it reads rows sequentially from disk instead of jumping around by index pointer.

An index hurts when the optimizer chooses it wrongly. Statistics can be stale, especially after a bulk load or a sudden shift in data distribution. The engine then estimates ten rows, uses the index, and reads a million.

An index hurts when it is never used. It still consumes disk, memory for caching, and write amplification. Unused indexes are common after schema changes or after a query pattern shifts.

An index hurts when there are too many. A table with twelve indexes turns every single-row insert into thirteen write operations: one for the table and one for each index. On a busy write workload that latency shows up in lock time and replication lag.

Composite indexes help only when the query uses a leftmost prefix. An index on `(last_name, first_name)` speeds `WHERE last_name = 'Smith'` and `WHERE last_name = 'Smith' AND first_name = 'John'`, but it does not speed `WHERE first_name = 'John'` alone.

Covering indexes help when they include all columns the query needs. The engine reads only the index pages and never fetches the heap row. But wider indexes use more pages and cache, so they help reads and hurt writes more.

The right index is one that removes enough reads to pay for its maintenance. The wrong index is one that the optimizer ignores, or one that saves a scan on a report but adds milliseconds to every insert.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The sender assigns each outgoing byte a sequence number. The receiver acknowledges the highest contiguous sequence number it has received in order. If a segment arrives out of order, the receiver holds it in a buffer and repeats the acknowledgment for the last in-order byte. The sender retransmits any byte that goes unacknowledged past its retransmission timeout, or after three duplicate acknowledgments suggest a gap. The receiver then fills the gap, advances the contiguous window, and delivers the now-ordered stream to the application.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions on shared data.

A race condition happens when two threads read and write the same memory at the same time and the result depends on the order of their steps. One thread may read a value, another may overwrite it, and the first may then write back a stale result. A mutex prevents this by letting only one thread enter a critical section at a time.

The mutex itself is a lock. A thread acquires the lock before it touches the shared data and releases the lock when it is done. While one thread holds the lock, other threads that try to acquire it block until it is released. This serializes access: the operations inside the critical section happen one after another, not in parallel.

A mutex does not protect data automatically. It protects only the data that every thread agrees to access through that lock. If one thread updates a variable without holding the mutex, the protection fails. The correctness depends on convention, not on the mutex alone.

A mutex also does not prevent deadlocks. If thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1, both wait forever. Ordering lock acquisition or using a single lock prevents this.

Mutexes are coarse. A single mutex around a large data structure can make threads queue and slow the program. Finer locks can help, but more locks add complexity and more ways to deadlock.

In short: a mutex enforces mutual exclusion so that only one thread at a time can operate on shared state, and that is what prevents races.

Garbage collection finds unused memory by tracing what the program can still reach.

The collector starts from a set of roots: local variables on thread stacks, global variables, CPU registers, and any handles the runtime keeps. These roots hold the only references the program can use directly. The collector walks from each root to every object it points to, then to every object those objects point to, and so on. Every object it reaches is marked as live.

Any object the walk never reaches is unused. The program has no path to it, so it cannot read or write it again. The collector reclaims that memory.

Reference counting is a different approach. Each object stores a count of incoming references. When a reference goes away, the count drops. When the count hits zero, the object is unused and the runtime frees it immediately. Reference counting misses cycles: two objects that point only to each other keep each other's count above zero even when nothing else points to them. A tracing collector handles cycles because it cares about reachability from roots, not counts.

Generational collectors exploit one fact: most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations. New objects go in a young generation, which the collector scans often. Objects that survive several collections move to an older generation, which the collector scans less often. This avoids repeatedly tracing long-lived data.

Some collectors run concurrently with the program. They mark objects while the program mutates references, so they need barriers to catch changes. Stop-the-world collectors pause all threads, trace the heap, then resume. The pause is simpler to implement but visible to the program.

The key distinction is reachability, not time since last use. An object the program can no longer touch is garbage, whether it was allocated a millisecond ago or an hour ago.

A race condition is a bug where the outcome depends on the exact order in which two threads run their steps.

Picture two clerks updating the same ledger. The ledger holds a balance of 100. Clerk A reads 100, adds 50, and intends to write 150. Clerk B reads 100 at the same moment, subtracts 30, and intends to write 70. A writes 150. B writes 70. The final balance is 70, but the correct result of 100 + 50 − 30 is 120. A's deposit vanished because B overwrote it.

The race happens in the gap between reading and writing. Each thread took the old value, changed it locally, and wrote back a stale result. The loser of the race lost their update.

A mutex prevents this by letting only one clerk touch the ledger at a time. The first clerk reads, adds, and writes before the second clerk starts. The result becomes deterministic: 120.

A CPU cache speeds a program by keeping recently used memory close to the core.

A modern CPU has three levels of cache: L1, L2, and L3. L1 sits inside each core and holds a few tens of kilobytes; it can deliver data in a handful of clock cycles. L2, also per core, is larger but slower. L3 is shared across cores and slower still, yet still far faster than main memory.

When a core reads a byte, the hardware first checks L1, then L2, then L3, then RAM. A hit in L1 costs about four cycles. A miss to main memory can cost hundreds. On a 3 GHz core, that is the difference between roughly one nanosecond and over a hundred.

Caches exploit locality. Temporal locality means a byte used once is likely to be used again soon. Spatial locality means a byte used is likely to be near another byte used soon. The cache therefore fetches not one byte but a whole cache line, typically 64 bytes, hoping the neighbors will be needed.

A loop that walks an array sequentially benefits because each 64-byte line loaded serves the next sixteen integer accesses. A loop that jumps through a linked list benefits less because each node may land in a different cache line and possibly a different page.

A cache miss still happens when the working set exceeds the cache size. A program that scans a gigabyte array cannot keep it all in a few megabytes of cache; most accesses go to RAM. The same happens with false sharing, where two threads write different variables that happen to share a 64-byte line, causing the cache to bounce the line between cores.

Prefetch hardware can hide latency by loading lines before the program asks, but only when the access pattern is predictable. Random access defeats it.

In short, a CPU cache converts repeated nearby memory access into fast on-chip reads instead of slow trips to RAM.

Idempotency means an API call produces the same result no matter how many times the client sends it.

A client sends `PUT /users/42` with the same payload twice. The first request updates the user. The second request updates the user to the same state. The database ends at the same place after one call or ten.

`GET` is naturally idempotent. Calling it once or five times returns the same resource, assuming nothing else changes it.

`POST /charges` is usually not idempotent. Send it twice and the server may create two charges. APIs add an idempotency key — a header the client supplies — so the server recognizes a duplicate and returns the first result instead of running again.

Idempotency matters when networks fail. A client never knows whether a lost response means the server skipped the request or only the reply vanished. With an idempotent call, the client can retry safely. Without it, retrying may double the effect.

Safe methods are a related idea. `GET`, `HEAD`, and `OPTIONS` should not change server state. Idempotent methods may change state, but repeating them does not change it further. `DELETE /users/42` is idempotent: the first call removes the user; later calls find nothing and report the same outcome.

The practical test is state, not response. A server may return `200` then `404` for repeated `DELETE` calls, yet the resource stays deleted. The operation is idempotent because the server state does not keep changing.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a hierarchy of servers, each one narrowing the search.

A browser or program starts with a resolver, usually run by the operating system or the local network. The resolver first checks its own cache. If the answer is there, it returns immediately.

If not, the resolver asks a root server. There are thirteen logical root servers, named A through M, and they know only one thing: where the top-level domain servers live. The resolver asks a root server for `example.com`. The root server replies: ask the `.com` servers.

The resolver then asks a `.com` server. That server knows which name servers hold the records for `example.com`. It replies with their addresses.

The resolver asks one of those name servers. That server holds the actual record for `example.com`, such as an A record pointing to `93.184.216.34`. It returns the address.

The resolver caches the answer and hands it to the browser. The whole chain usually takes milliseconds.

Each step uses UDP on port 53 for the query, though large replies fall back to TCP. Records carry a time-to-live, measured in seconds, that tells resolvers how long they may cache the answer before asking again.

If a name has a CNAME record, the resolver must follow the alias and look up the canonical name. If the query asks for an IPv6 address, it requests an AAAA record instead of an A record.

The system is distributed so no single server knows every name. Each server knows only the next step, and the steps together resolve the name.

A deadlock is a standoff between two or more threads, each holding a resource the others need and waiting for a resource the others hold.

Picture two trucks on a narrow bridge. Truck A owns the north half and waits for the south half. Truck B owns the south half and waits for the north half. Neither can move. Neither will back up. They stay there.

In a program, the resources are usually locks. Thread 1 acquires lock A and asks for lock B. Thread 2 acquires lock B and asks for lock A. Both wait forever. The program hangs.

One way to avoid this is to order the locks and always take them in the same sequence. If every thread that needs both A and B always acquires A first, then B, the circular wait cannot form. Thread 1 takes A, then asks for B. Thread 2 also wants A, but A is held, so it waits. Thread 1 finishes and releases both. Thread 2 proceeds. No circle, no deadlock.

Other methods exist: try to acquire all locks at once with a timeout, or use a single lock instead of many. But a fixed global lock order is the most common fix. It costs nothing at runtime and removes the cycle that causes the hang.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket chosen by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, the map has a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions by chaining. Each bucket holds a linked list or tree of entries that share that bucket. A lookup hashes the key, walks the list at that bucket, and compares keys until it finds a match. Java's `HashMap` uses linked lists and switches buckets to red-black trees when they grow past eight entries.

Open addressing handles collisions differently. It stores every entry inside the table array itself. When a slot is occupied, the probe sequence tries the next slot—linear, quadratic, or by a second hash—until it finds the key or an empty slot. Python's `dict` and Rust's `std::collections::HashMap` use variants of open addressing.

Load factor governs performance. Chained maps slow down as buckets lengthen; open-addressing maps degrade as clusters form. Resizing to a larger array and rehashing every entry restores the ratio. A well-distributed hash function keeps collisions rare; a poor one turns the map into a linear search regardless of the strategy.

A database index is a separate data structure that points to rows in a table so the database can find them without reading every row.

Most indexes are B-trees. The database keeps the indexed column values sorted in a tree of pages; a lookup descends from the root to a leaf, then follows a pointer to the row. A primary key index in PostgreSQL or InnoDB is a clustered index: the leaf pages contain the row itself. A secondary index stores the indexed columns plus a reference to the primary key.

Indexes speed up reads and some joins. They hurt writes, because every insert, update, or delete that touches an indexed column must also update every index. They hurt storage, because each index is a copy of part of the data. They hurt query planning when the optimizer chooses the wrong index or refuses to use one, such as when a query applies a function to the indexed column or compares with a leading wildcard.

An index also hurts when it is redundant. Two indexes on the same leading columns waste space and write overhead. A narrow index on a column with very low cardinality, like a boolean flag, may scan nearly as many rows as a table scan.

Indexes help most on large tables with selective queries that return a small fraction of the rows. They help least, or actively harm, on small tables, heavy write workloads, and queries that return most of the table anyway.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The receiver uses those numbers to reassemble the stream in the right order and to detect gaps.

Each TCP segment carries a sequence number for its first byte. The receiver acknowledges the next sequence number it expects. If segment 2 arrives before segment 1, the receiver holds it in a buffer and repeats the acknowledgment for 1 until 1 shows up. Once 1 arrives, TCP delivers both in order to the application.

The sender retransmits anything that goes unacknowledged past a timeout or after several duplicate acknowledgments. This fixes loss, which is the main cause of out-of-order delivery on the internet.

Flow control and congestion control keep the sender from overrunning the receiver or the network, but they do not reorder data. Ordering is the job of the sequence numbers, the receive buffer, and retransmission.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions when several threads share memory.

Only one thread can hold a mutex at a time. A thread locks the mutex before it reads or writes the shared data, then unlocks it when it is done. The next thread waits until the lock is free.

Without a mutex, two threads might read the same value, both add to it, and both write back a result that loses one update. A mutex makes the read-modify-write sequence atomic, so the final value is correct.

A mutex does not prevent deadlocks. If thread A locks mutex 1 and waits for mutex 2 while thread B holds mutex 2 and waits for mutex 1, both stall. It also does not stop a thread from accessing the data through a path that never locks the mutex.

A garbage collector finds unused memory by tracing reachable objects from a set of roots.

The roots are the places where the program currently holds references: local variables on thread stacks, global variables, and CPU registers. The collector starts at these roots and follows every pointer to an object. It marks each object it reaches.

After marking, the collector sweeps the heap. Any object without a mark is unreachable from the program and therefore safe to reclaim. The collector adds that memory back to its free list or returns it to the allocator.

Some collectors add a reference count to each object. The count rises when a new reference points to the object and falls when a reference disappears. When the count hits zero, the collector reclaims the object immediately. Reference counting cannot collect cycles: if object A points to B and B points to A, both counts stay above zero even when nothing else references them.

Generational collectors exploit the observation that most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations and trace the young generation more often than the old one. An object that survives several collections gets promoted to an older generation.

Tracing collection pauses the program while it walks the object graph. The length of the pause depends on the number of live objects, not the size of the heap. Incremental and concurrent collectors interleave tracing with program execution to shorten or eliminate these pauses.

A race condition is a bug where the result of a program depends on the exact timing of independent events.

Consider two threads that share a counter. The counter starts at 0. Each thread reads the value, adds 1, and writes it back. Thread A reads 0. Before A writes, thread B reads 0. Both write 1. The counter ends at 1 instead of 2.

The bug is not in either thread alone. It appears only when their operations interleave in a particular way. A mutex around the read-add-write sequence prevents it by making the sequence atomic.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping recently used memory close to the core.

Modern CPUs run at gigahertz, but main memory answers in tens to hundreds of nanoseconds. That gap is long enough for the core to execute hundreds of instructions while waiting. A cache is a small, fast memory bank between the core and RAM. It stores copies of memory locations the program has touched.

When the core reads an address, the cache checks first. A hit returns the data in a few cycles. A miss sends the request to RAM and stalls the pipeline. Caches work because programs reuse data: the same variable is read many times, and nearby memory is often accessed next. Hardware exploits this with lines, typically 64 bytes, fetched together, and with multiple levels—L1 fastest and smallest, L2 larger, L3 shared across cores.

A cache also speeds writes. A write-back cache stores the change locally and flushes to RAM later, avoiding a round trip on every store. When many cores share data, caches must keep copies consistent, usually with a coherence protocol such as MESI, which marks each line as modified, exclusive, shared, or invalid.

The speedup is not automatic. A program that jumps through memory randomly misses often and gains little. A program that walks arrays sequentially or reuses a small working set hits often and runs much faster.

Idempotency means the same HTTP request can run more than once without changing the result beyond the first run.

A `GET` request is idempotent by design. Calling it once returns the resource; calling it ten times returns the same resource and leaves the server state unchanged.

A `PUT` request replaces a resource. Sending it once sets the value to X. Sending it again sets the value to X. The second request does the same work, but the outcome does not differ from the first.

A `POST` request that creates a new order is usually not idempotent. Sending it twice creates two orders. A `DELETE` request is idempotent. Deleting a resource once removes it; deleting it again leaves it removed.

Idempotency matters when networks fail. A client may retry a request if it never sees a response. If the request is idempotent, the retry is safe. If it is not, the retry may duplicate an action.

HTTP methods signal idempotency. `GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `OPTIONS` are idempotent. `POST` and `PATCH` are not, unless the server implements them that way explicitly.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a chain of name servers.

A browser or application calls a stub resolver, usually inside the operating system. The stub resolver checks its cache. If the name is missing, it sends a query to a recursive resolver, often run by an ISP or a public service such as Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 or Google's 8.8.8.8.

The recursive resolver asks the root name servers. The roots do not know addresses; they point to the top-level domain servers for `.com`, `.org`, `.net`, and the rest. The resolver asks the TLD servers. They point to the authoritative name servers for the specific domain, such as `example.com`. The resolver asks those authoritative servers. They return the record that maps the name to an IP address.

Each answer carries a time-to-live value. The resolver caches the record for that many seconds and answers later queries from memory. If the record expires, the resolver repeats the chain.

A single query can return more than one record. An `A` record gives an IPv4 address. An `AAAA` record gives an IPv6 address. A `CNAME` record says the name is an alias and points the resolver at another name to look up.

The whole exchange usually takes one round trip from the client, because the recursive resolver has done the walking.

A deadlock is a standoff between two or more threads where each waits for a resource the other holds.

Imagine thread A locks a file and then tries to lock a database connection. Thread B already holds the database connection and is waiting for the file. Neither can proceed. Both sit forever unless something breaks the cycle.

One way to avoid it is lock ordering. Every thread acquires the same resources in the same order. If both A and B always lock the file before the database connection, B cannot hold the database while waiting for the file, and the cycle cannot form.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket chosen by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, the map has a collision.

Most hash maps chain colliding entries. Each bucket holds a linked list, and a lookup walks that list until it finds a matching key. Java's `HashMap` uses linked lists and switches them to balanced trees when a bucket grows past eight entries.

Open addressing handles collisions differently. It places entries directly in the table array; when a bucket is full, the probe continues to the next slot until it finds the key or an empty one. Python's `dict` and CPython's newer compact dict use a variant of open addressing with a separate dense array for values.

Load factor governs when the map resizes. A higher load factor saves memory but lengthens chains or probes; a lower one wastes space. Java resizes at 0.75. Resizing rehashes every entry into a larger table, which is the main cost of a growing hash map.

The hash function matters. A poor one clusters entries in a few buckets and turns the map into a slow list. Good implementations mix the key's bits, as in `hashCode ^ (hashCode >>> 16)`, to spread low bits across the table.

Average lookup, insert, and delete stay O(1) with a good hash and reasonable load. Worst case is O(n), when every key collides.

A database index is a separate structure that points to rows so the engine can find them without scanning the whole table.

Most indexes are B-trees. The database walks the tree by key value and reaches a leaf that stores the row's location or primary key. A lookup on an indexed column costs O(log n) page reads instead of O(n) row checks.

An index hurts when maintaining it costs more than it saves. Every insert, update, or delete must change the index too, so write-heavy tables with many indexes slow down. Indexes also consume disk space and memory; a large index may push working data out of cache.

Indexes fail to help when the query does not match them. A query with a function on the column, like `WHERE UPPER(name) = 'ALICE'`, cannot use a plain index on `name`. A query that returns most of the table may be faster with a full scan than with random index lookups. Composite indexes only help when the query uses a left prefix of the columns.

Covering indexes help reads because the index alone satisfies the query. Redundant or unused indexes hurt writes and storage without benefit. The query planner's choice depends on statistics; stale statistics can make it ignore a useful index or use a costly one.

In short, an index trades faster reads for slower writes and more space. It helps when it lets the engine touch fewer rows; it hurts when it adds work the query does not avoid.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The receiver uses those numbers to reassemble the stream in the right order and to detect gaps.

Each TCP segment carries a sequence number. That number marks the first byte in the segment's payload. The receiver acknowledges the next byte it expects, not the last one it got. If segment 1000–1999 arrives but 2000–2999 is missing, the receiver keeps acknowledging 2000 while it buffers the later segments that did arrive.

The sender keeps a window of unacknowledged bytes. It retransmits anything that stays unacknowledged past a timeout or after three duplicate acknowledgments for the same sequence number. That retransmission fills the gap without waiting for the original to time out.

The receiver delivers bytes to the application only once the stream is contiguous. Out-of-order data waits in the socket buffer until the missing piece arrives. This turns an unreliable packet network into an ordered byte stream.

A mutex protects a program against races on shared data.

A race happens when two threads read and write the same memory without ordering. Thread A checks a counter, thread B increments it, and thread A's update overwrites B's. The counter loses one increment.

A mutex enforces one thread at a time in a critical section. A thread locks the mutex before touching the shared data and unlocks it after. While one thread holds the lock, others block or spin until it releases.

The protected resource is the data, not the mutex itself. The mutex does not stop threads from running; it stops them from entering the guarded section together. If a thread forgets to lock, or locks the wrong mutex, the race returns.

Mutexes also prevent torn reads and writes. On a 32-bit machine, a thread might see half of a 64-bit update. A mutex makes the whole update atomic relative to other threads that use the same lock.

Deadlock is the main risk. Thread A locks mutex 1 and waits for mutex 2 while thread B holds mutex 2 and waits for mutex 1. Consistent lock order fixes this.

A mutex trades concurrency for correctness. It serializes access to shared state so threads see a coherent view.

Garbage collection starts from the roots: global variables, active stack frames, and CPU registers that hold references.

It marks every object reachable from those roots. If object A points to object B, B stays alive. The collector follows every pointer it finds and sets a mark bit on each object it reaches.

After marking, it sweeps. Any object without a mark bit is unreachable, so the collector reclaims its memory. This mark-and-sweep cycle runs when the allocator runs low on free space.

Reference counting is a different approach. Each object stores a count of incoming references. When a reference disappears, the count drops. When it hits zero, the object is dead. It cannot collect cycles: if A points to B and B points to A, both counts stay above zero even when nothing else references them.

Generational collectors exploit a real pattern. Most objects die young. New objects go in a nursery; survivors move to an older generation. The collector scans the nursery often and the old generation rarely, because the nursery yields far more garbage per scan.

Tracing collectors pause the program while they walk the heap. The length of the pause depends on live data, not dead data, because they must trace every reachable object. Incremental and concurrent collectors interleave marking with program execution to shorten pauses, at the cost of extra bookkeeping.

A race condition is a bug where a program's result depends on the timing or order of events that the programmer did not control.

Picture two threads sharing a single counter. The counter starts at 0. Each thread reads it, adds 1, and writes it back. Thread A reads 0. Before A writes, thread B reads 0 too. Both write 1. The counter ends at 1, not 2. One increment vanished.

The problem is the read-add-write sequence is not atomic. The operating system can switch threads between any two instructions. When the switch lands inside the sequence, the threads overlap instead of taking turns.

Race conditions also appear in file systems. Two processes check whether a temporary file exists, then both create it because each saw an empty slot. One process overwrites the other's work.

The fix is synchronization: a mutex, an atomic operation, or a design that keeps the data private to one thread. Without it, the program passes tests on a quiet machine and fails under load.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping copies of recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far from the CPU on a slower bus. A cache is a small, fast memory made of SRAM that sits between the CPU and RAM. When the CPU reads an address, the hardware first checks the cache. A hit returns the data in a few cycles; a miss fetches it from RAM and stores a whole cache line, typically 64 bytes, nearby.

Programs reuse data. They read the same variable twice, or walk an array in order. The cache exploits this with two patterns. Temporal locality means a recently touched address is likely to be touched again soon. Spatial locality means an address near a recent one is likely next. A cache line captures both by pulling in neighbors.

A modern CPU has multiple levels. L1 is smallest and fastest, often 32 KB per core and a few cycles. L2 is larger, perhaps 256 KB to 1 MB per core. L3 is shared across cores and can be tens of megabytes. Each level trades speed for size.

Cache misses cost hundreds of cycles. A program that jumps through memory randomly misses often and waits. A program that scans an array sequentially streams cache lines efficiently and runs faster on the same hardware.

The cache also helps writes. A write-back cache stores changes locally and flushes to RAM later, avoiding a round trip on every store. Coherence protocols keep multiple cores' caches consistent when they share memory.

In short, the cache works because fast, nearby memory beats a fast CPU waiting on distant RAM.

Idempotency means an API call produces the same result no matter how many times the client sends it.

A client sends a `PUT /users/42` with the same payload twice. The first request updates the user. The second request updates the user to the same state. The database ends in the same place, and the client receives the same response.

Safe methods are idempotent by definition. `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, and `TRACE` do not change server state, so repeating them changes nothing. `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent but not safe: they change state, yet doing them again leaves the state unchanged. `POST` is usually not idempotent; each `POST /charges` may create a new charge.

Idempotency keys let a server recognize retries. The client sends a unique key in the header. The server stores the result for that key and returns the stored response on repeats instead of re-running the work. Stripe uses this to prevent double charges when a network timeout makes the client retry.

The practical value is reliability across unreliable networks. A request may reach the server, change state, and then fail to return. The client cannot tell whether the change happened. An idempotent endpoint lets the client retry safely. Without idempotency, retries risk creating duplicate records or duplicate side effects.

Idempotency is about effect, not implementation. The server may log each request or update a timestamp; the visible state and the response to the client must stay the same.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a chain of resolvers.

A browser or app calls a stub resolver on the local machine. The stub resolver checks its cache. If the name is not there, it sends a query to a recursive resolver, usually run by the ISP or a public service like Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 or Google's 8.8.8.8.

The recursive resolver asks the root name servers. There are thirteen logical root servers, lettered A through M, and they know where the top-level domain servers live. The root server answers with the addresses of the servers for `.com`, `.org`, `.net`, or whatever the suffix is.

The recursive resolver then asks the TLD server. The TLD server knows the authoritative name servers for the specific domain. It returns their addresses.

The recursive resolver asks the authoritative server for the domain. That server holds the zone file, which maps `example.com` to an A record for an IPv4 address or an AAAA record for an IPv6 address. It may also return a CNAME, which points the resolver at another name to look up.

The recursive resolver caches the answer and returns the address to the stub resolver. The stub resolver caches it too. The browser opens a TCP connection to that address.

Each query and response uses UDP on port 53 for ordinary lookups, and TCP for large responses or zone transfers. A record carries a time-to-live, measured in seconds, that tells resolvers how long they may keep it before asking again.

A deadlock is a standoff between threads. Each one holds a lock the other needs, and neither can move.

Picture two bank accounts and two threads. Thread A locks account 1 and waits for account 2. Thread B locks account 2 and waits for account 1. Both sit forever.

One fix is a fixed lock order. Always lock the lower-numbered account first. Both threads then compete for account 1 first; one wins, takes account 2, finishes, and releases. The other follows. No circle forms.

They hurt when they fragment. Repeated updates and deletes leave the B-tree sparse, so scans touch more pages than the data needs. Rebuilding or reorganizing the index compacts it again.

The right index is one that removes enough full-table scans to pay for the writes it adds.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The receiver uses those numbers to reassemble the stream in the right order and to detect gaps.

Each segment carries a sequence number. The receiver acknowledges the next expected number with `ACK`. If segment 3 arrives before segment 2, the receiver holds 3 in a buffer and repeats `ACK` for 2 until 2 shows up. Once 2 arrives, TCP releases 2 and 3 to the application in order.

The sender retransmits anything it does not get an `ACK` for within its retransmission timeout. That timeout is not fixed; TCP measures the round trip and adjusts it.

The window size tells the sender how much data the receiver can buffer. The sender keeps unacknowledged bytes in flight below that limit. This prevents overrun while still allowing multiple segments to travel at once.

Selective acknowledgment, `SACK`, lets the receiver list specific missing blocks instead of just the lowest one. The sender then retransmits only those blocks, not everything after the gap.

Sequence numbers wrap around at 2³² bytes. Protection against ambiguity from old segments comes from the timestamp option and from the receive window, not from a larger number space.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions on shared data.

Only one thread can hold the mutex at a time. When a thread wants to read or write shared memory, it locks the mutex first. If another thread already holds the lock, the caller waits until the lock is free.

Without this guard, two threads could read the same value, both add one, and both write back the same result. The counter would increase by one instead of two. The mutex makes the read-increment-write sequence atomic from the program's point of view.

A mutex does not prevent deadlocks. If thread A locks mutex 1 and waits for mutex 2 while thread B holds mutex 2 and waits for mutex 1, both wait forever. Programmers avoid this by locking resources in a fixed order.

A mutex also does not protect against a thread accessing the data without locking. Every path that touches the shared state must take the lock; one forgotten path breaks the protection.

A garbage collector finds unused memory by tracing what the program can still reach.

It starts from roots: local variables on thread stacks, global variables, and CPU registers that hold references. These roots point to objects in the heap. The collector follows each reference recursively, marking every object it touches.

Any object the mark phase does not reach is unreachable from the running program. The collector sweeps those objects and reclaims their memory.

Reference counting is a different approach. Each object stores a count of incoming references. When a reference disappears, the count drops. When it hits zero, the object is dead. This misses cycles: two objects that point only to each other keep each other's count above zero even when nothing else references them.

Generational collectors exploit a pattern called the generational hypothesis: most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations and scan the young generation more often, moving survivors to older generations. This reduces the work of each collection.

A tracing collector must pause the program or coordinate with it so object references do not move while it walks them. Concurrent and incremental collectors interleave collection with program execution to shorten those pauses.

A race condition is a bug where the result of a program depends on the exact timing of independent operations.

Consider two threads that increment the same counter. Each thread reads the counter, adds one, and writes it back. Thread A reads 10. Before A writes, the scheduler pauses A and runs thread B. B reads 10, writes 11, and finishes. A resumes, writes 11, and finishes. The counter ends at 11 even though two increments ran.

The bug is not that the threads ran at the same time; it is that their read-modify-write steps interleaved. A mutex or atomic increment fixes it by making the sequence indivisible.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far from the cores on a slower bus. A cache is a small, fast bank of SRAM between the core and RAM. When the CPU reads an address, the hardware first checks the cache. A hit returns the data in a few cycles; a miss fetches a whole cache line, typically 64 bytes, from RAM and stores it for reuse.

Programs spend much of their time in loops and repeated access patterns. The cache exploits two of these. Temporal locality means an address used once is likely to be used again soon. Spatial locality means nearby addresses are likely to be used next. Loading a whole line captures both.

Caches are layered. A modern CPU has a private L1 cache split into data and instructions, a larger private L2, and a shared L3. L1 is fastest and smallest; L3 is slower but holds more. The core checks L1, then L2, then L3, then RAM.

A cache speeds a program only when the working set fits. If the program jumps through memory randomly or touches more data than the cache holds, misses dominate and performance drops close to RAM speed. Tight loops over small arrays run fast because they stay in cache.

Idempotency means the same HTTP request can be sent more than once without changing the result beyond the first time.

A client might retry a `PUT /users/42` because the first call timed out. If the request is idempotent, the server ends up with the same user data whether the call ran once or three times. The second and third requests do not create extra users or corrupt the record.

`GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` are normally idempotent. Calling `GET /orders/7` ten times returns the same order. Calling `DELETE /orders/7` ten times leaves the order deleted; the first call removes it, and the rest report that it is gone.

`POST` is usually not idempotent. A retry of `POST /orders` can create two orders if the server already processed the first request. APIs sometimes add an idempotency key header so the server can recognize a duplicate `POST` and return the original response instead of creating another resource.

The guarantee helps clients recover from network failures. Without it, a retry risks double booking, double charging, or duplicate records.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a chain of name servers.

A browser or program sends the name, such as `example.com`, to a resolver. The resolver first checks its cache. If the answer is not there, it asks a root server. The root server does not know the address, but it points the resolver to the server for the `.com` zone. The `.com` server points the resolver to the authoritative server for `example.com`. That server returns the A record, which holds the IPv4 address, or the AAAA record for IPv6.

Each answer has a time-to-live value. The resolver caches it for that many seconds and answers later queries from memory.

If the name has a CNAME record, the resolver follows the alias and looks up the canonical name. If the query asks for a mail server, the resolver returns the MX record, which names the host that accepts mail for the domain.

The whole exchange usually finishes in milliseconds because most names are cached at the resolver, the operating system, or the browser.

A deadlock is a standoff between threads or processes that each hold a resource the other needs.

Thread A locks the account-balance mutex and waits for the transaction-log mutex. Thread B locks the transaction-log mutex and waits for the account-balance mutex. Neither releases what it has, so both wait forever.

One fix is a global lock order. Every thread that needs both mutexes must lock the account-balance mutex first and the transaction-log mutex second. Thread B, which wanted them in the opposite order, now takes them in the same order as A. The cycle cannot form, because no thread can hold the second lock while waiting for the first.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket numbered by the key's hash code. Two keys can land in the same bucket; that is a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions by chaining. Each bucket holds a linked list. When a new key hashes to an occupied bucket, the map appends the pair to that list. Lookup walks the list and compares keys with `equals` until it finds a match.

Open addressing is the other common method. It stores every entry inside the table array itself. When a bucket is full, the probe continues to the next slot—linear, quadratic, or by a second hash—until it finds an empty one. Lookup follows the same probe sequence.

Chaining keeps performance predictable when the load factor grows, at the cost of pointer overhead per entry. Open addressing uses less memory but clusters as the table fills, so it needs a lower load factor and periodic resizing.

Resizing is the real fix: when the ratio of entries to buckets exceeds a threshold, the map allocates a larger array, recomputes every hash, and redistributes the entries. A good hash function and a prime or power-of-two table size keep collisions sparse.

A database index is a separate structure that points to rows so the engine can find them without reading the whole table.

Most indexes are B-trees. The database keeps the indexed column values sorted in a tree of pages; each leaf page holds pointers to the actual row locations. A query on an indexed column walks the tree in a few page reads instead of scanning every row.

An index hurts when maintaining it costs more than it saves. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` on the indexed column must update the index too, which adds writes and can split pages. A table with many indexes writes slowly.

An index also hurts when the query does not use it. If a query filters by an unindexed expression, or returns most of the table, the engine may ignore the index and scan anyway; then the index only consumes disk and memory.

Indexes hurt when they are redundant. Two indexes on the same leading column, or an index that duplicates another with a subset of columns, waste space and slow writes without helping reads.

Indexes hurt when they are too wide. An index that includes many long columns takes more pages, so fewer entries fit in memory and lookups touch more disk.

Finally, an index hurts when it exists for a query that almost never runs. The write penalty is paid constantly; the read benefit is paid rarely.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The sender puts a sequence number on each segment; the receiver uses that number to put the bytes back in order and to detect gaps.

The receiver sends acknowledgments that name the next byte it expects. If a segment arrives out of order, the receiver holds it in a buffer until the missing bytes show up. It does not deliver data to the application until the stream is contiguous.

The sender keeps a copy of everything unacknowledged. When an acknowledgment is missing for too long, or when it sees three duplicate acknowledgments for the same sequence number, it retransmits the lost segment.

A sliding window limits how much data can be in flight at once. The receiver advertises how much buffer space it has left; the sender sends no more than that. This prevents the receiver from being overrun and gives TCP a way to pace retransmissions without flooding the network.

The result is a single ordered byte stream rebuilt from segments that may arrive scrambled, duplicated, or not at all.

Without this guard, two threads can read the same value, both change it, and both write back. One update disappears. A thread can also read a value while another thread is halfway through writing it and see a half-formed state.

A mutex does not stop threads from running. It only orders their access to the protected region. The region must be small and the same lock must guard every access to the same data, or the protection fails.

Deadlock is the cost. If thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1, both stop forever. A consistent lock order, or fewer locks, prevents this.

A race condition is a bug that appears when two threads use the same data at the same time and the outcome depends on which thread wins.

Picture two clerks updating the same ledger. Each reads the balance, adds a deposit, and writes the new total. Clerk A reads $100. Clerk B reads $100 before Clerk A writes back. Both add $50 and both write $150. The real total should be $200, but one deposit vanished.

The program did not crash. It produced the wrong answer because the two read-modify-write steps overlapped. A mutex, an atomic increment, or a compare-and-swap would force the updates to run one at a time and keep the balance correct.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping recently used memory close to the processor.

The CPU fetches data from main memory in small blocks called cache lines, typically 64 bytes. When the program reads a byte, the CPU brings the whole line into the cache. The next access to that line reads from fast SRAM instead of slow DRAM.

Caches exploit two patterns. Temporal locality means a program reuses the same data soon. Spatial locality means it touches nearby addresses next. A loop that sums an array benefits from both: the same counter repeats, and the array elements sit next to each other.

A cache hit reads in a few cycles. A miss stalls the pipeline for hundreds of cycles while main memory responds. Good code keeps the working set small and walks memory sequentially. Scattershot pointer chasing thrashes the cache and turns hits into misses.

Multiple cache levels trade speed for size. L1 sits on the core and holds 32 to 64 KB. L2 and L3 are larger and shared. The CPU searches L1 first, then L2, then L3, then RAM. Each deeper level is slower but catches more.

False sharing is the trap. Two cores write different variables that happen to live on the same cache line. Each write invalidates the other core's copy, forcing both to refetch from memory. Padding variables to separate cache lines fixes it.

A cache does not help a program with no locality. It rewards code that reuses what it already loaded.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a hierarchy of servers.

A browser or program starts with a stub resolver on the local machine. The stub does not know the answer, so it sends the name to a recursive resolver, usually run by the operating system or the network provider.

The recursive resolver asks the root servers. The roots do not know `www.example.com`, but they know which servers handle `.com`. The resolver asks a `.com` server. That server points to the name servers for `example.com`. The resolver asks one of those. The authoritative server for `example.com` returns the A record, which holds the IPv4 address, or the AAAA record for IPv6.

If the name is a CNAME, the resolver follows the alias and repeats the lookup for the canonical name. If the query asks for mail, it returns an MX record pointing to a mail server instead of an address.

A deadlock is a standoff between threads. Each holds a resource the other needs, and neither can move.

Picture two trucks on a narrow bridge. Truck A enters from the north and blocks the southbound lane. Truck B enters from the south and blocks the northbound lane. Both wait for the other to back up. Neither does. They stay there.

In a program, the trucks are threads and the bridge lanes are locks. Thread 1 locks account A and waits for account B. Thread 2 already locked account B and waits for account A. Both wait forever.

One way to avoid it is a fixed lock order. Every thread that needs both accounts must lock account A before account B. Thread 2 would then take A first, finish its work, and release both locks before Thread 1 needs them. No circle forms, so no one waits in vain.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket numbered by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, the map has a collision.

Most hash maps chain colliding entries. Each bucket holds a linked list, or in Java's `HashMap` since Java 8, a tree if the list grows long. The map inserts the new entry at the head or tail of that bucket's list. Lookups scan the list and compare keys with `equals()` to find the right one.

Open addressing handles collisions differently. It places the entry in the next empty slot, probing forward by a fixed step or by quadratic increments. Python's `dict` and CPython's compact dict use a variant of open addressing with a separate index array.

Load factor governs when the map resizes. As the table fills, collisions cluster and lookups slow. Resizing creates a larger array and rehashes every entry into new buckets.

The choice of hash function matters. A poor function maps many keys to the same bucket and turns every lookup into a linear scan. A good function spreads keys evenly across the table.

Separate chaining keeps insertion simple and handles any number of collisions. Open addressing uses less memory but degrades badly when the table gets full.

A database index is a separate data structure that points to rows in a table, built on one or more columns so the database can find values without scanning every row.

Most indexes are B-trees. The database keeps the indexed column values sorted in a balanced tree of pages, each page a fixed-size block on disk. A lookup walks from the root to a leaf, then follows a pointer to the row. A B-tree keeps the height low, so even a billion-row table needs only a few disk reads.

An index helps when the query filters, joins, or orders on the indexed column. It also helps enforce uniqueness and foreign keys. A covering index, one that includes all columns the query needs, lets the database answer from the index alone and skip the table.

An index hurts when it is unused but maintained. Every insert, update, or delete on the table must update every index on that table. That costs disk writes and locks. Wide indexes, with many included columns, magnify the cost. Indexes also consume disk space and memory; large ones can push useful data out of cache.

An index can hurt query performance too. If the query returns many rows, the database may read the index and then the table for each matching row, which is slower than a full table scan. The optimizer sometimes chooses a full scan because the index would not narrow the result enough. A selective predicate, one that eliminates most rows, makes the index worthwhile; a predicate that returns half the table does not.

Indexes also fail when the query does not match their shape. A leading-column rule applies to composite indexes: an index on `(last_name, first_name)` helps a filter on `last_name` alone, but not a filter on `first_name` alone. Functions and implicit conversions on the indexed column can prevent the database from using the index.

In short, an index trades faster reads for slower writes and more storage. It pays off when it lets the database touch fewer rows.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The sender assigns each byte a sequence number. The receiver acknowledges the highest contiguous sequence number it has received. The sender retransmits any byte that the receiver has not acknowledged within a timeout.

The receiver uses the sequence numbers to reassemble data in the right order. If a packet arrives out of order, the receiver holds it in a buffer until the missing bytes show up. It does not deliver data to the application until the gap closes.

The receiver sends duplicate acknowledgments for the last in-order byte it received. Three duplicate acknowledgments usually trigger a fast retransmit at the sender, which resends the missing segment without waiting for the timeout.

The sender also keeps a congestion window and a receive window. It sends new data only when both windows allow it. This pacing prevents the network from overflowing and keeps the ordered byte stream intact.

A mutex protects a program against the wrong result when several threads touch the same data at once.

A thread must lock the mutex before it enters the critical section. Only one thread can hold the lock at a time. Other threads that try to lock it block until the holder unlocks it. This serializes access to the shared resource.

Without a mutex, two threads can read, modify, and write the same value in overlapping steps. A race condition follows: the final value depends on which thread wins, and the program can lose updates, corrupt a structure, or break an invariant.

A mutex does not prevent deadlock by itself. If thread A locks mutex 1 and waits for mutex 2 while thread B holds mutex 2 and waits for mutex 1, both stall. Programmers avoid this by locking resources in a fixed order.

A mutex also does not fix every concurrency problem. It guards shared state, but it does not make a computation atomic across multiple independent operations unless the programmer wraps all of them in the same lock.

A garbage collector starts from the roots: global variables, CPU registers, and the frames on each thread's stack. It marks every object the roots can reach, then reclaims everything it did not mark.

Tracing collectors follow references recursively. If object A points to object B, and A is alive, B stays alive. The collector builds this reachable set and treats the rest as dead.

Reference counting keeps a tally of incoming pointers instead. When the count drops to zero, the object is unused and the collector frees it immediately. Cycles break this: two objects that point only to each other keep each other alive even when nothing else references them.

Generational collectors exploit a real pattern. Most objects die young, so the collector scans the young generation often and the old generation rarely. Objects that survive several young collections move to the old generation.

Mark-sweep collectors pause the program, mark live objects, then sweep the heap and free the unmarked blocks. Mark-compact collectors also move live objects together, which removes fragmentation but takes more time.

Incremental and concurrent collectors interleave work with the program to shorten pauses. They track changes the program makes while collection runs, so newly created or modified references do not hide live objects.

The collector cannot reclaim an object the program can still reach through any pointer. Memory leaks happen when the program keeps references it no longer needs.

A race condition is a bug where a program's result depends on the timing or order of independent operations.

Picture two threads in a ticket system. Each thread reads the count of remaining seats, subtracts one, and writes the count back. Thread A reads 10. Before A writes 9, thread B also reads 10. Both threads write 9. Two seats were sold, but the count dropped by one.

The threads did not coordinate. Each acted on a stale value because the read and write were not atomic. The final state is wrong, and the exact result changes from run to run.

A race condition needs three things: shared data, at least two threads or processes that touch it, and at least one write. Reads alone do not race. A write and a read, or two writes, can.

The fix is to make the operation atomic. A mutex, an atomic increment, or a database transaction can force the threads to take turns. Then the second thread sees the result of the first, not the old value.

A CPU cache speeds a program by keeping recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far from the cores, on separate chips reached through a bus. A load from DRAM can take a hundred nanoseconds or more. The cache is a smaller, faster memory made of SRAM on the same chip as the CPU. A load that hits the L1 cache completes in a few cycles.

Programs reuse data. They read the same variable twice, or walk an array in order, or call the same function repeatedly. The cache copies those bytes from DRAM into lines, typically 64 bytes each. The next access finds the data nearby.

Caches are layered. L1 is smallest and fastest, often 32 to 64 kilobytes per core. L2 is larger and slower, shared or per-core. L3 is larger still and shared across the chip. A hit in a closer level avoids the longer trip to the next.

Spatial locality helps. When the cache fetches one byte, it pulls the whole line. A loop that reads array elements in order hits the cache on most iterations. Temporal locality helps too. A variable used in one statement and used again soon stays in the cache.

A cache miss costs time. The CPU stalls while it fetches from a deeper level or from DRAM. Good programs arrange their work so that each loaded line gets used many times before it is evicted.

Idempotency means an HTTP request can run more than once without changing the result beyond the first run.

A client sends a `PUT` to update a user's email. The server applies the change and returns `200 OK`. If the network drops and the client retries the same `PUT`, the email stays the new value. It does not flip back and forth, and it does not create a second copy of the user.

The same holds for a `DELETE`. The first call removes the resource and returns `204 No Content`. A second `DELETE` to the same URL finds nothing and returns the same `204`. The resource remains gone.

`GET` and `HEAD` are idempotent by nature. They only read state. Calling them again returns the same representation, assuming nothing else has changed it.

`POST` is usually not idempotent. A `POST` to `/orders` creates a new order each time it runs. Retry the same `POST` twice and the server makes two orders.

Idempotency matters when networks fail. TCP can retransmit, clients can retry, and proxies can replay. An idempotent method lets the client resend without asking the server what happened first.

Servers signal success the same way on the first and later calls. A repeated `PUT` returns `200` or `204`. A repeated `DELETE` returns `204` or `404`. The body may differ, but the resource state does not drift.

Idempotency is a promise about effect, not about response. Two identical `GET` calls may return different data if another client changed the resource between them. The method is still idempotent because the calls themselves did not change anything.

DNS translates a hostname into an IP address through a chain of delegated lookups.

A browser or application first checks its own cache. If the name is not there, it asks a recursive resolver, usually run by the operating system or the local network. The resolver checks its cache too. If it still lacks the answer, it starts from the root.

The resolver queries one of the root name servers. The root does not know the final address. It returns the addresses of the servers for the top-level domain, such as `.com` or `.org`.

The resolver then asks a top-level domain server. That server does not know the final address either. It returns the addresses of the authoritative servers for the domain, such as `example.com`.

The resolver asks an authoritative server for `example.com`. That server holds the record that maps `www.example.com` to an IP address. It returns the A record for IPv4 or the AAAA record for IPv6.

The resolver caches the result and hands it back to the application. The application opens a connection to that IP address.

Each zone delegates authority downward. The root delegates `.com`. The `.com` servers delegate `example.com`. The `example.com` servers answer for hosts inside it. This hierarchy lets DNS scale without any single server knowing every name.

Caching shortens the process. Records carry a time-to-live, measured in seconds. Resolvers reuse cached answers until that timer expires, which reduces traffic and speeds repeated lookups.

A deadlock is a standoff between two or more threads, each holding a resource the others need and waiting for a resource the others hold.

Picture two clerks and two files. Clerk A has the payroll file and needs the inventory file. Clerk B has the inventory file and needs the payroll file. Neither will release what they have until they get what they want. Both wait forever.

One way to avoid this is to lock resources in a fixed order. Every thread that needs both mutex A and mutex B must lock A first, then B. No thread can lock B before A. The circular wait disappears, and the deadlock cannot form.

This rule works only when the program can name a global order. If locks are created dynamically or buried inside libraries, the programmer must still arrange them so that every path through the code acquires them in the same sequence.

Deletion in open addressing needs a tombstone marker so that probes can still find entries inserted after the deleted one. Separate chaining deletes by unlinking the node, with no tombstone needed.

A database index is a separate, ordered copy of a column or columns that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table.

They hurt when they cover the wrong columns. An index on `(last_name)` cannot satisfy a `WHERE` clause on `first_name`; the database must still scan.

They hurt when there are too many of them. A table with a dozen indexes pays that write penalty twelve times over.

They hurt on small tables, where a sequential scan is already fast and the index adds lookup overhead.

They hurt when statistics are stale, because the query planner may choose the index for a result set that is larger than expected, triggering many random disk reads instead of one sequential pass.

In short: an index trades faster reads for slower writes and more storage. It pays off only when it lets the database skip enough work.

The receiver sends acknowledgments back. Each acknowledgment names the next sequence number it still needs. Gaps in the sequence tell the sender which bytes got lost.

The sender retransmits missing segments. It keeps a copy of everything unacknowledged in its retransmission queue until the receiver confirms receipt.

This keeps the byte stream ordered end-to-end even when packets take different paths, arrive out of order, or drop and need resending.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions on shared data.

A race condition happens when two threads read and write the same memory at the same time. One thread can overwrite another's change, or two threads can read a stale value and both base their next write on it.

A mutex is a lock. One thread acquires it before touching the shared data. While that thread holds the lock, other threads that try to acquire it block until the lock is released. Only one thread at a time enters the protected section.

This makes operations on the shared data atomic from the program's point of view. A thread can read a value, modify it, and write it back without another thread stepping in between.

A mutex does not protect against deadlocks on its own. If thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1, both wait forever. Ordering lock acquisition prevents that.

It also does not protect against bugs inside the critical section. If a thread modifies the data wrongly, the mutex merely keeps other threads out while it does so.

A garbage collector finds unused memory by tracing reachable objects from known starting points.

The collector begins at roots: local variables on thread stacks, global variables, and CPU registers that hold references. These roots point directly to objects the program can use right now.

It follows each reference outward. If object A references object B, the collector marks B as reachable and follows B's references in turn. This walk covers the whole object graph the program can reach.

Anything the walk never reaches is garbage. The program has no path to that object through variables, fields, or collections, so it cannot use it again. The collector reclaims that memory.

Reference counting is a different approach. Each object stores a count of incoming references. When the count drops to zero, the object is unreachable and its memory is freed. Reference counting cannot collect cycles: if object X points to Y and Y points back to X, both counts stay above zero even when nothing else points to either.

Generational collectors exploit a observed fact: most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations and scan the young generation more often, since that is where most garbage appears.

A tracing collector pauses the program while it walks the graph, or it runs concurrently and tracks references that change during the scan. Either way, the goal is the same: keep what the program can reach, discard the rest.

A race condition is a bug that appears when two threads touch the same data at overlapping times and the outcome depends on the order their instructions run.

Picture two cashiers sharing one ledger. Each reads the balance, adds a deposit, and writes the new total. Cashier A reads $100. Before A writes, cashier B reads the same $100. A writes $120. B writes $130. B's write overwrites A's, and $20 disappears.

The program did not crash. Both threads ran valid code. The result was wrong because the reads and writes interleaved in one particular way. A different scheduling order would have produced the correct $130.

A race condition is not the same as a deadlock. A deadlock stops threads because each waits for a lock the other holds. A race condition lets threads run and corrupts data instead.

The fix is to make the read-modify-write sequence atomic. A mutex around the ledger forces one cashier to finish before the other starts. Atomic instructions on the CPU can do the same for single operations. Either way, the goal is to remove the timing-dependent interleaving.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping copies of recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far from the CPU on a separate chip, and a fetch from it can take hundreds of clock cycles. The cache is smaller SRAM on the same die or package; a hit there costs only a few cycles.

Programs tend to reuse the same data and instructions soon after touching them. This is temporal locality. They also tend to read nearby memory together, which is spatial locality. The cache exploits both.

When the CPU reads a byte, the cache fetches a whole block, called a cache line, typically 64 bytes. Later reads to the same line hit the cache instead of main memory.

Caches are layered. A modern CPU has a small, fast L1 cache per core, a larger L2, and a shared L3. A request checks L1, then L2, then L3, then RAM. Each miss costs more, but each layer is bigger.

Writes are cached too. A write-back cache stores the change locally and flushes to main memory only when the line is evicted. A write-through cache updates both at once.

Cache misses still happen. A cold miss occurs on first access. A capacity miss happens when the working set exceeds the cache size. A conflict miss happens when too many addresses map to the same cache set and evict each other.

Good performance comes from fitting the hot data and code into the cache and accessing it in predictable patterns. A loop that strides through an array sequentially runs fast; the same loop jumping by large powers of two can thrash the cache.

Idempotency means an API call produces the same result no matter how many times the client sends it.

A `GET` request is idempotent by nature. Calling it once or ten times returns the same resource, assuming nothing else changes it.

A `PUT` to `/users/123` with a fixed payload is idempotent. The first call sets the name to "Alice." The second call sets the name to "Alice" again. The server state matches the request, so repetition does not pile up changes.

A `POST` to `/charges` is usually not idempotent. Each call creates a new charge. Retry a failed `POST` twice and the customer may be billed twice.

Idempotency matters for retries. Networks drop packets, clients time out, and the server may process a request without the client ever seeing the response. An idempotent endpoint lets the client retry safely.

APIs often enforce idempotency on non-idempotent methods with an `Idempotency-Key` header. The server stores the key with the result of the first request and returns the same result for repeats, without running the operation again.

The guarantee is about effect, not response code. A retry may return `200` while the first call returned `201`, but the underlying state change happens once.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a chain of name servers, each one closer to the answer.

A browser or program starts with a resolver, usually run by the operating system or the local network. The resolver checks its cache first. If it has no record, it asks a root server.

The root server does not know the address. It points the resolver to the server for the top-level domain, such as `.com` or `.org`.

The top-level server does not know the address either. It points the resolver to the authoritative server for the specific domain, such as `example.com`.

The authoritative server holds the actual record. It returns the IP address for the name.

Each answer has a time-to-live value. The resolver keeps the record in its cache until that time expires, then asks again.

If a name maps to multiple addresses, the resolver may return them in rotation. If the authoritative server returns a `CNAME`, the resolver follows the alias and asks again for the canonical name.

The whole exchange usually takes a few UDP packets and finishes in milliseconds.

A deadlock is a standoff between threads that each hold a resource the other needs.

Thread A locks the account table and waits for the transaction log. Thread B locks the transaction log and waits for the account table. Neither releases what it has. Neither gets what it needs. Both wait forever.

One way to avoid it is to make every thread acquire locks in the same order. If both threads always lock the account table before the transaction log, then B cannot hold the log while waiting for the table, and A cannot hold the table while waiting for the log. The cycle cannot form.

This rule works only when the system can enforce a global lock order. If some code paths cannot know all locks in advance, or if locks come from different modules, ordering them is harder. In those cases timeouts, lock hierarchies, or avoiding locks entirely may be necessary.

A hash map stores each key-value pair at an index produced by a hash function. When two keys hash to the same index, the map has a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions by chaining or open addressing. Chaining keeps a linked list or tree at each bucket; every entry that hashes to the same index goes into that structure. Open addressing probes other slots in the array, checking linear, quadratic, or double-hash offsets until it finds an empty one.

The load factor governs performance. As the ratio of entries to buckets rises, collisions cluster, so the map resizes to a larger array and rehashes all entries.

A good hash function spreads keys uniformly, which keeps collisions rare; a poor one clusters them and degrades lookups to linear scans.

A database index is a separate structure that points to rows so the engine can find them without scanning the whole table.

Most indexes use a B-tree. The engine walks the tree by key value and reaches a leaf that stores row identifiers or pointers. A lookup that would read every row instead reads a few pages.

An index helps when the query filters, joins, or sorts on the indexed column. It also helps enforce uniqueness and foreign keys, because the engine can check existence quickly.

An index hurts in three common ways.

First, it costs space. The index file holds a copy of the indexed columns plus pointers. On a write-heavy table, every insert, update, or delete must update both the table and every index. That slows writes.

Second, it can make a query slower. If the query returns most of the table, reading the index and then fetching rows one by one is more work than a full table scan. The optimizer may choose the index anyway if its cost estimate is wrong.

Third, it adds maintenance. Indexes fragment, statistics go stale, and the query plan can degrade until someone rebuilds or updates them.

So an index is a trade-off: faster reads for slower writes and more storage. It pays off when queries use it to avoid large scans; it wastes resources when they do not.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The sender puts a sequence number on each segment; the receiver uses that number to reassemble the stream in the right order.

If a segment arrives out of order, the receiver holds it in a buffer and waits for the missing piece. It sends duplicate acknowledgments for the last in-order byte it received, telling the sender exactly what gap to fill.

The sender retransmits the missing segment when it notices the gap — either from three duplicate ACKs or when a retransmission timer expires. Once the missing bytes arrive, the receiver releases the buffered segments in order and advances the window.

This sequence-and-acknowledge scheme also detects loss and prevents the receiver from passing a scrambled stream to the application.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions on shared data.

A race condition happens when two threads read and write the same memory at the same time. Without a mutex, one thread can overwrite another's work, or two threads can read a stale value and both write back a wrong result.

A mutex solves this by letting only one thread enter a critical section at a time. The thread that wants the data calls `lock`. If another thread already holds the mutex, the caller waits. When the owner finishes, it calls `unlock`, and the next waiting thread proceeds.

This mutual exclusion keeps updates atomic from the program's point of view. It does not prevent deadlocks on its own; if threads lock multiple mutexes in different orders, they can wait on each other forever. It also does not make code faster; it serializes access, which can slow a program when contention is high.

A mutex is the right tool when several threads must touch the same variable or structure and at least one of them writes. It is the wrong tool when threads do not share state, because the lock would add overhead for no benefit.
